#8721. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!)

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

This realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”)

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.)

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#8717. The Best Triathlon Suits of 2026, Tested by Real-World Triathletes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Best tri suits of 2026 rated and reviewed based on 10 criteria. (Photo: Triathlete)

Men's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

Women's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

When you look good, you feel good – and when you feel good, you race great. It’s no surprise, then, that when triathletes gear up for race day, they spend hours looking online for the best tri suit.

Indeed, in our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, 88% of respondents said aesthetics were at least “somewhat” important, with 38% saying they wouldn’t wear what they felt was an “ugly” kit.

But a great triathlon suit is more than good-looking – ideally, it also needs to fit well, carry your nutrition stash, provide an aero- and hydro-dynamic advantage, and protect the tender bits from chafing.

We’re asking a lot of tri suits these days, but the industry has stepped up to the challenge. Legacy brands like Zoot and Coeur, as well as newcomers Ryzon and Tri-Fit, have made it possible for triathletes to find not only a suit that meets their practical race-day needs but also shows off their own personal style.

With so many options available, we asked the Philly Tri Club and Triathlete contributors to help with real-world testing of the top triathlon suits of 2026. The 150-strong club is all about creating an inclusive training community, and club members in a variety of shapes and sizes put tri suits through the paces, wearing them through workouts and races and making note of what works and what doesn’t in their triathlon kit reviews. Here’s what they had to say about the best triathlon suits of 2026.

In our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, we asked readers what brands of triathlon apparel they had in their closets. Though more than 20 brands were represented, the top six are familiar names in the industry.

Pockets: 2 back pockets, 2 svelte front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

The Regna Elite Trisuit offers a custom fit via an app that completes an AI-powered body scan for a fit based on your unique features. For the ultimate test, we tasked Triathlete contributor Jon Dorn and his wife Heather with testing it out. Jon stands at 6’6” and is self-described as very slender. His wife is 5’3” “buxom, and more powerfully built,” according to Jon.

“I’ve finally found a tri suit that doesn’t chafe my ass or distract me as various sensitive parts start smarting,” said Jon.

Heather noted that the suit was a 95% perfect fit, though the midsection was slightly loose. As someone who doesn’t fit into the “one-size-fits-most” size structure, she was still quite pleased. “This is the best my undercarriage has felt in a tri kit in years,” she reported after a four-hour training ride.

Ultimately, the pair found that the price tag is the biggest deterrent and only really justifiable if you’re someone who doesn’t fit into a standard tri kit well.

If you’re looking for a budget triathlon suit for a sprint or Olympic triathlon that won’t chafe, the 2XU Core Tri Suit is a safe bet. It lacks adequate padding and pockets sizable enough to carry enough nutrition for long-course training or racing, but at the $200 price point, it’s a rare find for short-course racing.

It’s light on compression if that’s your preference and when it comes to breathability, the suit was disappointing, so ideally plan to wear it in more forgiving weather, as our tester found that it trapped heat and sweat more than other comparable suits.

Our tester found it hard to criticize anything about this suit because it fit snugly and comfortably. While she doesn’t normally wear sleeved tri suits, she was pleasantly surprised by how thin and breathable the fabric on these sleeves was, to the point that she forgot the sleeves were even there.

The tri suit has ample compression, especially in the core. The one detractor is that this suit only comes in black or black and white, which is a little generic and not as fun as some of the other options on this list. User beware, too: our tester noticed a bit of color leaking when handwashing the suit. Consider wearing the suit for shorter training sessions or wearing a belt with additional fuel, as the two back pockets are medium-sized and diagonally aligned.

Pockets: 3 back pockets, 2 inner front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

When it comes to tri suits, it’s the little details that make a brand stand out. In this case, Tri-Fit’s attention to pockets – six in total, including one explicitly for holding ice on your neck during hot races – is reason enough to consider the Vortex for a long-course race.

Testers liked the fit, fabric choice, design, pockets, and overall feel, noting that it looks great with small logos, lightweight fabric, and comfortable chamois padding for shorter events. The chest zips up tightly, preventing wind trap, and performed well during rides and runs.

However, there was substantial drag in the water, and the vent holes under the arms caused chafing – vented fabric would be preferable, as would slightly more compression on the legs. In all, however, the Tri Fit feels premium, and with a few minor design tweaks, could quickly become a favorite tri suit.

Pockets: 1 lower-back channel pocket, 1 neck ice pocket

This tri suit performed adequately in the heat, thanks to the use of smart temp technology, which dials up evaporation from the skin to the air as body temperature rises. The super-thin and light chamois also mitigates heat well, especially on long rides, and strategically-placed airflow channels on the shoulders and back help things feel cool and fast on the bike.

However, the top zipper rubbed against the chest, causing discomfort during running and biking. It also chafed at the neckline due to the lack of a zipper cover. Testers liked that it fit well, but disliked that the zipper needed a fabric cover and that the white top was see-through, especially when wet coming out of the swim or sweating on the run (women testers noted their sports bra was visible while wearing the suit in a race).

At $125, Black Bibs brand has created a budget-friendly triathlon suit that stands out in a market full of offerings $300 or more. But “budget” should not be conflated with “cheap” here – the suit fits well, provides exceptional compression, and is a classic style (men’s and women’s one-piece colorways include a solid black as well as a black bottom half with navy, burgundy, or white uppers). Openings for the legs and arms use silicone “power bands” to keep the suit secure throughout a workout or race, and no chafing was reported. The suit also proved extremely durable both on and off the race course, holding up through dozens of laundry cycles without shrinking, pilling, or splitting seams.

The initial impression of the chamois was mediocre, but improved with subsequent use and resolved itself after several rides. Testers reported drag when swimming, with the neckline sagging, and recommended use with a wetsuit. Dislikes included poor moisture wicking, especially in the upper body, and unusually high rear pockets.

Unlike some tri brands, where women’s suits are simply a smaller version of the men’s, Coeur tri suits are designed with a woman’s physique in mind, from the contours of the suit to the women’s specific seamless chamois. Testers also liked the supple fabric and one-piece design with a full front zipper and high-rise short beneath, allowing for breathability and extra roominess in the torso.

This tri suit performed exceptionally well on the swim and run, but some chafing was experienced on the bike – chamois cream is recommended. The arm openings run slightly small, so athletes with muscular arms should size up or opt for the sleeveless version. Luckily, Coeur offers a variety of competitively-priced women’s tri suit configurations in matching colorways: sleeved, sleeveless, sports bra/shorts, aero tops, and tri tops with built-in bras.

Testers liked the sleek, minimalist, and professional appearance of the monochromatic Arise tri suit, as well as its stretchy, comfortable, and “slippery” feel that allowed for movement and flexibility without chafing. It remained comfortable even when wet, ran true to size, didn’t create unnecessary drag, and worked well with other clothing. This tri suit generally performed well across all conditions and disciplines, with no reported poor performance or chafing.

However, a dime-sized hole appeared in the left armpit after two wears, which was surprising and disappointing, given the suit’s $335 price tag. Testers also wished the back pocket was deeper and had multiple compartments.

Pockets: 1 rear pocket, two side pockets, 3 interior pockets

Zoot has been a mainstay of triathlon apparel for more than 40 years, and for good reason – users recognize the balance of form and function present in many of its products. The suits, designed by endurance athletes, for endurance athletes, come in a variety of designs, including flashy patterns and colorways.

The latest offering from Zoot, the Ultra Tri P1, performed well during swims in the ocean, bike rides on a trainer and outside, and runs outside. Testers liked its comfortable and true-to-size fit as well as built-in UPF 35 sun protection fabric.

However, the pockets were not very big, making it difficult to carry proper nutrition during training rides or runs – testers recommended wearing the suit for short-course racing or long-course events only if nutrition on the course is plentiful. The zipper was also annoying and rubbed a bit, requiring multiple adjustments while running.

Overall, however, the suit was rated as “top-notch” for comfort, breathability, and weight.

(Photo: Thomas Barwick | Getty; All in Motion; Canva)

Looking for the best inexpensive yoga mats? With the following picks from our expert testers, you’ll experience more than sufficient grip and cushiness while keeping to a budget. The standouts are the Gaiam Premium 5mm Yoga Mat ($24), which is the best yoga mat for beginners, and the All in Motion Peak Rubber Yoga Mat ($35) for the best overall inexpensive yoga mat, especially for hot yoga. Whether you’re new to yoga or simply don’t want to spend a lot of money, these are the most reliable options to consider.

No one talks about this. But you can experience some serious B-rated horror movie moments when you practice on a lot of yoga mats. Your hands slowly and inexorably sliding forward as you try to find stillness in Down Dog. Your mat wrinkling and sliding beneath you as you attempt to transition from Low Lunge into Warrior 2. It’s enough to make you want to silently and helplessly scream.

You would think that throwing money at the problem helps. And I’m not gonna lie, sometimes it can when you splurge on stand-out yoga mats that support you in ways that are unspeakably better than other mats. But not every absurdly expensive mat ensures you avoid these cringe situations. Just as not every inexpensive mat guarantees you’ll experience challenges. And not everyone wants to or is able to spend a lot of money on a mat. And until you’ve actually practiced on a mat, it’s pretty much impossible to discern what it’s like.

So we did the testing for you. I spent the first decade of my yoga practice on a $17 mat quite similar to one of the selections below, and throughout the next decade of my yoga practice, I’ve slipped, slided, and sweated my way through poses on dozens of different yoga mats in all price ranges, and so have our other testers of all experience levels. In so doing, we’ve culled the options for spending less than $50 down to the two most reliable, decidedly non-nightmarish, unequivocally best inexpensive yoga mats.

Because you don’t need to let price deter you from your practice, whether you’re a beginner or simply someone who thinks of everything else you could put that extra money toward (ie your electric bill, groceries, those vintage 90s cargo pants on Poshmark that you can’t stop thinking about). You just need to avoid the ones that make you question your decision to try yoga. Instead, you should simply be questioning your discretion in choosing a mat.

Here’s everything you need to know to make the right decision.

Material: Latex-free PVC Thickness: 5mm Dimensions: 68 x 24 inches Weight: 2.6 pounds

Pros and Cons + Sufficiently sturdy, grippy + cushy + Ethereally lightweight + Price! – Slightly slippery, especially when wet – Smaller dimensions than most mats

This is what you buy when you want to spend as little as possible on a mat that delivers rather than disappoints. Not surprisingly, it’s from longtime mat maker Gaiam, which offers dozens of styles, although the Premium 5mm is my choice for its textured surface, decent enough traction for hands and feet even during arm balancing, and spongy cushiness that lets you sink ever so slightly into the mat.

Although it’s not as densely cushioned as most more expensive mats, the Premium 5mm was preferred by beginners who found the texture to be reassuringly supportive during standing postures and sufficiently comfortable during shapes that require kneeling, sitting, or reclining. That said, if you think you’ll practice primarily yin or restorative yoga, in which you’re sitting or lying on your mat the entire class, you might want something cushier.

Look, it’s not flawless. In testing during recent years, it sometimes wrinkled slightly beneath my feet as I transitioned, although not in an overly distracting way. It sometimes felt as though my hands or feet were beginning to slide on the slick surface, but not to the extreme experienced on other mats in this price category. Although when practiced on during heated or sweaty conditions, that slide factor increased, so consider yourself warned. As for longevity, if you end up practicing several times a week, the mat might show signs of the surface wearing down wherever you commonly place hands and feet, although Gaiam does offer a lifetime guarantee.

Whatever the mat lacks in longevity, it more than makes up for in lightweightness. At just 2.6 pounds, it’s easy to lug along with you to class, even if you walk several city blocks to a studio or gym. (Trust me, pricier mats get heavy quite quickly.) Part of that seeming weightlessness might be due to the fact that it’s a couple inches narrower than a lot of mats, making for a slightly constricted experience in terms of square footage beneath you during your practice.

The mat is made of PVC. Some retailers refer to the material as “non-toxic,” which might sound like an anomaly. Gaiam’s website states it is made without the phthalates DEHP, DBP, BBP, DINP, DIDP and DNOP.

This is almost the same Gaiam mat that I started practicing on years ago, and although I haven’t used the ones I’ve tried in recent years for as long, at some point they, too, seem to start showing signs of wear in places where I regularly place my hands and feet. I don’t regret having chosen Gaiam and I strongly encourage others do the same. But if I had to do it again, I’d know when to let it go.

Bottom Line: It’s an inexpensive yoga mat that’s ideal for anyone curious to try yoga but not certain if they’ll want to stick with it in the long run. Or someone who practices occasionally, whether at home or at a studio or gym. Or as a suitable stand-in for someone who’s still deciding what, exactly, they prefer in a pricier mat before making that commitment.

Material: Polyurethane + rubber Thickness: 5mm Dimensions: 68 x 26 inches Weight: TK

Pros and Cons + Grippy surface + Doesn’t wrinkle or slide on the floor + Comparable to mats twice its cost – Heavy – Surface scratches easily

The Peak has a sleek surface, quite similar to that of more expensive brands designed for hot yoga that cost exponentially more. (IYKYK.) If I didn’t know better, I’d guess it cost closer to $100 based on how well it handles during my intermittent usage of it during vinyasa practices the last couple years.

The mat literally did not budge beneath me during any sort of transition in between poses thanks to its rubber base that practically adhered the hardwood floor beneath it. And don’t be fooled by that smooth polyurethane surface, because it capably held my hands and feet in place, even when sweating or in a heated space.

The mat also brings a dense cushiness, one that doesn’t feel spongy, unstable, imbalanced, or anything other than supportive and amply comfortable for seated and reclined poses. I’ve practiced yin yoga on it and had no complaints.

It is heavy, though. So you probably want to commute with it in the trunk rather than carrying it along sidewalks. And that sleek surface doesn’t remain unscathed if, like me, you have four-pawed friends who like to stretch their claws beneath you while you’re in Down Dog or Warrior 2. But the rest of the mat is as rugged as its heft would suggest. Mine has no signs of breaking down so far.

Bottom Line: When you want durability or just a decent grip to see you through any style of practice, this is the most acceptable mat priced below $50.

Not surprisingly, there are caveats for any inexpensive yoga mat that costs less than $50. So depending on how you practice, perhaps you think of the mat as one that’s “enough.” As in, cushy enough. Grippy enough. Supportive enough. And good enough to keep you from being distracted by what’s happening beneath you as you practice. Because as much as I appreciate the way these mats handle for the money, they are not designed the same as mats that cost exponentially more. Adjust your expectations accordingly.

Also, and importantly, neither of these mats is an altogether sustainable option. (With my sincerest apologies to the planet.) If eco-friendly options are a priority for you, rest assured, you can find an array of yoga mats, although most are in the $60-plus realm.

Consider, though, that sustainability can be defined in several ways. If either of the above mats meets your short-term needs yet ultimately ends up being your starter mat rather than your long-term mat, you can always donate it to a local school, community center, studio, or thrift store and let it become someone else’s starter mat. That, too, is sustainability. Or if that mat has become worn in ways you wouldn’t want to practice on, neither will someone else. In that case, repurpose it around the house or donate it to a local animal shelter.

Three years ago, we looked beyond the mats we typically practice on and canvassed online comments from users for dozens and dozens of brands of yoga mats of all price points. Then we asked 18 yoga students and teachers of all experience levels with yoga to try various yoga mats that received the highest ratings. And each year since then, we look to see which mats are surging in popularity or new to the market and test those as well. This year, we took special interest in budget options that might not have made our list of overall best, and took into consideration our experience while standing, transitioning, balancing, kneeling, sitting, and reclining on several mats.

#8711. Inside the 24-Hour World Record Attempt That Raised Over $500K+ for a Local Food Bank

Ethan Hunger attempts to break the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons in 24 hours. (Photo: Grayson Baum/Minus 7, Inc)

Beating the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons completed in 24 hours was the goal of my friend Ethan Hunger’s annual community fundraising event. But the record itself was really only a small part of it. The attempt was just one piece of his much bigger, yearlong goal to raise $500,000 for our local food bank – a fundraiser that has been growing through various endurance challenges since 2021.

The idea for his annual “Hunger vs. Hunger” fundraiser was born out of the COVID-related growth of food insecurity in his local area of Bellingham, Washington. What started as a one-year challenge that raised $30,000 has now amassed a total of $1.2 million in donations, and this year’s $500,000 challenge would equate to roughly 7% of the food bank’s annual budget.

The concept and message Ethan shares through these extreme challenges is simple: “No matter how hard a day I create for myself, it will never parallel the struggles of food insecurity.”

For year six, Hunger wanted to go bigger than ever, and a triathlon world record would certainly tick that box while also adding more eyes to the cause. Initially, the record sounded relatively simple when the idea came to light: swim, bike, run, and transition continuously for 24 straight hours – non-stop through the entire night – and beat the previous record of 18 complete triathlons. (Technically, Guinness records the attempt in legs, so he needed 55 completed to surpass the previous record).

However, it quickly became more challenging throughout the buildup. The logistics of putting on a “race” like this at a public park while also adhering to more than 30 pages of Guinness rules began to set in – and that was before considering the largest fundraising goal Hunger had ever attempted.

Here’s how it all unfolded: the behind-the-scenes difficulties of a Guinness World Record, what 24 hours of triathlon actually felt like, how the fundraiser brought it all together, and why he might have stumbled on a revolutionary triathlon idea.

There is a massive difference between saying you broke a world record and having Guinness officially verify it. During the buildup, we found the endless list of verification rules a bit redundant and overly complicated. However, they create a rigorous, no-corner-cutting environment that helps maintain the integrity of the records.

Still, we wished it didn’t cost an estimated $14,000 to send an adjudicator to verify our attempt on-site – which would’ve made everything a lot easier.

Hunger applied for the records six months in advance and was approved. Not everyone gets this approval, as part of the application involves demonstrating that you not only have the experience and skills to attempt something like this, but also the connections and know-how to pull off the necessary verification.

Guinness has a lot of requirements before ratifying an attempt: video, timing, GPS files, logs, photos, and documentation for seemingly everything. So in a feat nothing short of a miracle, we scrambled together seven main cameras to record for 24 hours straight, three additional dedicated cameramen for an upcoming documentary, multiple photographers, timing data, and GPS tracking. But despite all that, one requirement quickly became much more problematic than the others: witnesses.

We discovered late that an individual witness could only cover a four-hour period before needing a four-hour break. We were also further limited in who could qualify, so close friends and family couldn’t simply fill every opening (as we had initially planned).

So, less than a week before a 24-hour event, on top of figuring out nutrition, bikes, course logistics, lights, cameras, batteries, timing, and how the hell any of us planned to stay awake for 24 hours, Ethan now needed to find people willing to stand beside a lake, jump in a safety car for the bike, and on mountain bikes for the run at ridiculous hours of the night and officially confirm that he was, in fact, doing the correct distances.

“If I had to pick one thing that made the event coordination the hardest, it was the witnesses and their four-hour time constraint,” Hunger says.

Somehow, through social media and word of mouth, people volunteered. They came out at midnight, early in the morning, and at all sorts of inconvenient hours. Some of them didn’t know Ethan at all – they simply heard what he was trying to do and wanted to help.

That should have been our first indication of what this event was eventually going to become. The world record might have been Ethan’s, but a lot of people were beginning to feel like they had a small piece of it.

By the end of his record, Hunger had amassed 5.47 miles of swimming, 136.7 miles of biking, and 34.2 miles of running. Yet those numbers are not what he will remember.

I asked him what stands out the most, and his answer goes back to minute one. It paints a picture of the day perfectly:

“The one that lingered for me the longest was likely the starting line. I had been frantically running around for 20 hours trying to get everything set up. I ran over to the start line with my goggles and swim cap, and I looked around with 60 seconds left and finally had the moment sink in of all the incredible people who were there to support me. I saw an older gentleman who I used to volunteer with at the food bank, who I knew had driven 30 minutes to town just to see me start. I saw friends who had flown from around the country. I saw people who currently work at the food bank who came to cheer, and I saw friends who currently rely on the food bank who came to cheer. It was incredibly moving.”

He might have been the one whose name would be attached to the attempt and record, but very quickly it stopped feeling like something he was doing alone. That came partly from the decision to use a real course. From a logistical standpoint, doing the challenge at a pool and track would have been infinitely easier to film, manage, illuminate, and monitor. Every time we left transition on the bike or run course, we disappeared from the main event area, which made everything more complicated.

“There were a ton of moving parts to this, and so many of them were out of my control once the clock started,” Hunger said. “I was able to do my best to get it set up ahead of time and put people in charge of tasks, but then I had to be willing to let it go and hope that it worked out.”

And it did work out: People were joining in on the swim, bike, and run legs throughout almost every reasonable hour (staying behind Ethan to avoid drafting). There was a DJ playing music, food, a campfire, friends sitting around talking, people donating, and strangers coming down simply because they’d heard something ridiculous was happening. Because the distances were short, people could also participate without committing to an enormous endurance challenge of their own. Someone could join one swim, somebody else could do four runs, and others could ride a bunch of the bike legs. Because every leg eventually returned to the same transition area, the group kept coming back together again.

That made the atmosphere completely different from a traditional long-distance triathlon where an athlete might disappear for several hours. If Ethan left on the bike, everyone knew he’d be back in around 25 minutes. If somebody wanted to join the next run, they had a good idea of when it would start.

It helped break the endless cycle of triathlon feeling like such an individual sport and started to feel more like a 24-hour triathlon festival.

We had no idea going in what to expect physically. We’d only practiced this format for about six hours, none of us were truly trained as ultra-triathletes, and sure, we’d completed an Ironman before, but we all safely assumed that somewhere around hour 12 or 15 our bodies would start falling apart.

Weirdly, however, that wasn’t really what happened. Because every individual leg was short and we weren’t moving particularly fast, you’d finish a swim, bike, and run and think, That actually wasn’t too bad. The problem was overcoming the sleep fatigue and the dread of doing specific legs again (and again) with so many hours still ahead.

“My lowest moment was around 3 or 3:30 in the morning,” Ethan says. “I had just finished a triathlon where I was cold the entire time, and I was incredibly sleepy, too. The wind was still causing chop on the lake, and we had headwinds on our bike ride out. I just remember dreading going back in the water because I was already cold, and I knew when I finished the swim, and the wind hit me on the beach, I’d instantly be cold again.”

There were many other smaller obstacles along the way, too. One of which stands out for its irony. Hunger had spent a lot of effort organizing with Outbound Lighting to help illuminate the docks and buoys, to make the night swim one of the coolest parts of the whole experience, yet, in a synchronous moment of shared disbelief, we realized we all had forgotten clear-lens goggles.

On the bike, going from wet to cold to warm meant clothes never quite dried, while chafing, tired hands, wind, darkness, and some sketchy late-night traffic (picture drunk drivers yelling out the window) slowly added up.

Despite that, the hardest part for me might have been the small act of leaving the transition itself: even in the middle of the night, there was a campfire, music, food, and people hanging out, and sitting down beside that fire and prolonging the transition was all too enticing.

Maybe the best way to picture the mental struggle of this challenge is to imagine doing 15 hours of triathlon, getting to 9 a.m. when the sun was finally up, feeling like you’ve survived the hard part – then realizing you still have nine hours left.

For something that had taken 24 hours, the finish felt surprisingly quick. There were lots of people, lots of emotion, and we were all incredibly proud of Ethan. After 22 complete super-sprint triathlons, four more than the previous record, it was finally over.

Then we quickly cleaned everything up and headed to a big party, where Ethan somehow managed to give a speech in front of a few hundred people gathered to celebrate what it was all actually for. The Foodbank.

The number is already over the $500,000 goal, and with still much of the year left, and a documentary release still to come, that should have him far surpassing his expectations.

If you want to donate, you can do so here.

He describes just how much it means to the organization that now helps feed almost 5,000 families weekly in our county:

“My fundraiser is big enough and has been around long enough that the food bank now builds this fundraiser into its annual projection for income. If you combine that with the 2025 federal budget cuts that cost the Bellingham Food Bank around $900,000 and food banks across the country well over $1 billion, the need is there now more than ever.”

There are times when attempting a world record can appear outwardly selfish, done for vanity, to gain attention, or to level up your status. Ethan even received some comments on social media saying so, despite the clear purpose behind the fundraiser. But when you were on-site, you realized there wasn’t much glory in slogging through an attempt like this, and if you dealt with the months of buildup and preparation, you would quickly realize it probably wasn’t worth doing purely for the token of a Guinness stamp.

But doing it for a purpose, and with friends and a community around, made it all worth it. The record gave everyone something ridiculous to rally around; it gave hope, gave purpose, and made every small act feel like it was contributing to something much bigger.

Speaking of bigger, Ethan has already planned next year’s challenge: a 100-mile run around our local track and stadium.

#8710. Everything You Need to Know About Safely Practicing Standing Forward Bend

(Photo: Andrew Clark | Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Standing Forward Bend first appeared in the May-June 2001 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

In most contemporary societies, we are frequently exposed to confrontation—in our environments, in our relationships, in our jobs. When we lack the tools to deal skillfully with confrontation, our systems begin to contract—mentally, emotionally, and physically. When ignored for too long this contraction can color the way we perceive our “reality.” What is very unnatural to a healthy body can begin to seem natural.

Because this process occurs over extended periods of time, like the aging process, we often lack the awareness that it is happening until we are beyond simple fixes. With recognition and practice, though, this contraction can be used to create the “in-tense(ness)” necessary to overcome distortions in perception, enabling us to view confrontation as a useful, often necessary, component of growth.

Consider Uttanasana (Standing Forward Bend). If you are a beginner, whether you are stiff or flexible, this pose will likely take your attention directly into areas of your body that are unfamiliar, painful, and/or unresponsive. Stiff practitioners have to learn to work with pain, which is often intense, in order to remove obstructions found in the legs and hips in this pose. Less flexible beginners often struggle with the opposing forces of particular actions in a pose when they first encounter it. Attempting to relax muscles is not easy when you are receiving a steady stream (or scream) of more demanding messages in the seemingly undecipherable language of pain. It may feel like the resistance you experience is protecting you from injury or “overdoing.”

The Sanskrit word ut can be defined as intense but also as a point of indicated deliberation. By its very nature (and its name), Uttanasana takes us on a confrontational journey toward overcoming ingrained resistance and penetrating the dense matter of our consciousness. For those with chronically tight hamstrings and/or hips, the pose forces the mind into a very alert state and fills the “gaps” typically found in a beginner’s attention. This is a very important place to be. In it, you are given an opportunity to feel the physical power and observe the dynamics of a stressful situation, and to overcome the mental or emotional struggle inherent in that predicament.

Entering the pose requires a little preparation, and in the event of pre-existing lower back conditions, a couple of modifications may also be beneficial. If you practice in the early morning, it’s a good idea to get the spine warmed up first. (A little hot water focused on your spine for a few minutes in the shower can never hurt, although your utility bills might ache a little.) A simple way to set up the spine for forward bending in Uttanasana is to sit first in a cross-legged position and bend forward. This should give the hips a wake-up call.

From the sitting position, move into Downward-Facing Dog, which begins the process of lengthening the back of the legs and continues the work of elongating the spine. From Down Dog, with an exhalation, step or jump your feet to your hands, and as you inhale, slowly straighten your legs, keeping your hands on the floor. Lift your spine as you gaze forward. Feel the inhalation fill the back of your lungs, and as the back lungs and ribs expand, let the sensation of this lift support the movement in your thoracic spine.

As the spine lifts, feel a downward pressure on the hips and, catching that sensation, press the top of the hip bones (iliac crest) down firmly.

As you exhale, release your head and the weight of your shoulders completely and slowly shift your hips forward until you feel the balls of your feet taking your weight. Be careful not to move quickly, as this will often cause the heels to lift and the toes to grip the floor. Apply a downward pressure from the top of the knees down into the heels to help keep them on the floor.

The hands should rest on the floor beside or behind your feet with the fingers pointing forward. If the mobility of your hamstrings is limited and your hands don’t reach the floor easily, rest your palms on the front of your shinbones, with your legs straight. If the lower back is vulnerable to injury, take the feet hip-width apart, with your heels slightly wider than your big toes. Initially, don’t push with your arms to try to extend the spine. Let the movement of your inhalation into the back of your lungs create the subtle pressure to lift the weight of the spine softly, then surrender the weight of your spine on the exhalation. Notice the tendency for the hips to shift back and the weight to sink onto the heels with each cycle of breath. Constantly check to see how your weight is distributed and keep returning its force onto the balls of the feet.

As you begin to feel the subtle influence of the breath on the movement of the spine, notice the release of the exhalation, when the ribs are sinking and the diaphragm is soft. At this moment, flexible beginners whose hands reach the floor can extend from the top of the forearms, pressing into the palms, spread the shoulder blades, and elongate the spine from the back of the skull. The work of the arms should be in response to the movement in the spine—not the other way around. The intensity of the pose should build slowly from positioning and rhythmic breathing and never through excessive muscular force of the arms.

After holding the pose for five to 10 cycles of breath, slowly lift the spine on an inhalation, drawing the navel in slightly. If you’re coming up with tight buttocks and a gripped diaphragm, the lower back is vulnerable. Keep the buttocks and diaphragm passive, keep the legs straight, and allow the head to come up last, until you are standing in an upright position, arms resting at your sides.

Uttanasana, once mastered, allows for the understanding necessary for more advanced seated forward bends and beginning inversions. It helps build the digestive fire and, at the same time, is useful for rejuvenating the nervous system. With patient, persistent practice, Uttanasana will strengthen your mental focus and build your confidence as the confrontation found initially in the pose transforms into intelligence.

#8708. How Yin Yoga Bananasana Can Transform Your Swimming

Swimmers spend plenty of time working on stroke mechanics and building upper-body strength, but mobility of the side body, particularly the intercostal muscles between the ribs, can affect how freely you can breathe, especially as fatigue sets in.

Bananasana, a gentle yin yoga pose, stretches the side body. A supported side-lying pose, with blocks under the ribs and head, creates a more targeted stretch that can help expand your ribs for three-dimensional breathing.

While Bananasana offers a relatively subtle lateral stretch of the obliques, intercostal muscles, and IT band, a supported side-lying variation increases the sensation and may help ease fascial tightness.

Fascia is a network of connective tissue that surrounds and connects muscles, nerves, bones, and organs. When fascia’s layers glide well, the body moves freely. However, training load, injury, prolonged postures, and other factors can contribute to stiffness or reduced mobility. Restriction in the rib cage and side body can make a full, expansive breath feel harder to achieve.

Give your shoulders and lats attention, but don’t overlook your ribs and side body. Add these stretches to your regular mobility routine to build breath awareness and find more ease and efficiency in the water.

#8706. Camel Pose Helps Build Balance, Strength, and Flexibility

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Camel Pose first appeared in the September-October 2001 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

When looking at the meanings of the names of yoga asanas, especially those named after animals, you can find clues—sometimes literal and other times only suggestive —about the nature of the pose. With Camel Pose (Ustrasana) it’s a little of both.

What was it about this pose that inspired yogis of ages past to name it after the camel? Only by strenuously stretching the imagination can we find any resemblance to a healthy backbend in the shape of this animal.

Anatomically a camel’s body appears to be an assemblage of odd, unrelated parts, and the hump—the most unique and obvious characteristic—looks almost like an afterthought. Although camel humps may appear to be part of the spine, they are actually sacks of fat used to store partially digested food for long journeys. Through centuries of Asian and African civilization, the camel has also had a reputation for being a stubborn, ill-tempered animal with a serious lack of intelligence. Since it’s doubtful that the ancient yogis aspired to the image of lifting the spine like a camel hump, and a camel’s temperament is not exactly something to emulate in one’s yoga practice, why is this posed called the “camel”?

Traditionally the camel’s presence in the desert, one of the most inhospitable environments on our planet, has been one of the primary forces sustaining human life there. Though a camel’s eyesight is not keen, it relies on some inner compass to navigate its way through the desert. Used primarily as pack animals, camels instinctively know if a load is too heavy to endure over a long journey or if the weight is improperly balanced —and will refuse to move until the load is adjusted. Without a road map, in constantly changing surroundings of drifting sands, camels have the ability to read the signs and find the oases of green where water is present and food at hand.

Looking at the Camel Pose, we can begin to see a parallel. For many beginners, the “environment” in backbends is equally inhospitable. In general, beginning to bend backward is difficult and sometimes frightening, yet backbends are essential to maintaining a healthy spine. Generally we function in a forward-facing, right-side-up world, relying heavily on our eyes for our sense of identity and direction. In Camel, we must learn to cultivate another way of seeing. The shape of the pose places the head and one’s vision behind the body. It is an alien experience; our view of the world is literally turned upside down.

Our normal context for relating to ourselves and the image that sustains us is lost. For the beginner, a common reaction to the fear that comes from this loss of context is to shorten or hold the breath.

In addition, beginners often habitually contract the muscles of the buttocks and abdomen. The neck, if weak, becomes vulnerable as the shoulders grip for protection. When these reactions are present in the body, the movement in this pose does not respond well, especially if the student uses excessive muscular force. The pose feels out of balance, and the more we struggle, the less the pose responds. This only deepens the frustration, and we are likely to shut down or check out.

Basically there are two techniques for entering Camel Pose safely: dropping in from an upright kneeling position or lifting up from a seated position. Once you master these approaches in Camel Pose, a foundation has been laid for approaching the more advanced backbend Wheel Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana) either by lifting up from the floor or by dropping back from a standing position.

I recommend dropping in from the kneeling position in Camel for your first attempt if your lower back or knees are sensitive. This approach also works with gravity to help you avoid the natural tendencies of the beginner to overdo muscular effort. Begin by kneeling on your mat with your torso upright and the thighs perpendicular to the floor. Place your legs hip-width apart, with the tops of the feet flat on the floor and your arms at your sides. If your lower back is weak, place your hands on your buttocks to give more support to the lumbar spine as you enter the pose. Let your shoulders hang from the sides of your neck and drop your collarbones away from your ears. Initially keep your head upright, with your chin drawn slightly in toward the center of the throat. As you inhale, feel the fullness of your breath feeding the back, rather than the chest.

With each exhalation, let the weight of your chest and abdominal organs sink, as you keep the spine engaged upward from the back of the skull. Visualize the energy of the pose looping down along the front of the body (from the chest down through the hips to the shinbones on the floor) and up along the back of the body (through the spine to the crown of the head). Slowly take your head back; keep the throat soft and the shoulders down and slightly forward, with the shoulder blades broad. Avoid hardening the buttocks or the abdomen. Keep the top of the hips pressing firmly down into the knees, and as you bend the spine backward, let your arms hang from your shoulders with your fingers reaching back to touch the heels.

If the stress is excessive in your lower back, inhale back to an upright position, and after resting for a moment, try the pose again. Once your hands reach your feet, maintain the downward pressure from the top of the hip bones pressing into the knees, continue releasing the chest and abdomen down, and feel the lift from the floor into the thoracic spine.

The head should hang freely, with the neck supported by the width of the trapezius muscle along the top of the shoulders. The breath should remain slow and rhythmic, and with each exhalation, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, inhale back to an upright position.

Lifting up from the seated position can be more accessible when the neck is weak, but it tends to stress the legs and knees more intensely than the first approach, due to the fact that you are working against gravity. If your knees are weak, take care not to overstress them. And be patient—if your knees and groins are tight, you may not achieve full extension in the pose at first.

From an upright kneeling position, sit between your heels (use a block between your feet if necessary, with the palms of your hands placed on your heels, fingers pointing back. Slowly lean back, straightening your arms, taking your weight onto your hands, and lift your hips upward.

Press the shoulders forward, broaden the shoulder blades, and let the neck rest in the trapezius muscle as you take the head slowly back. As the hips lift upward and more weight is taken onto the lower legs, press the tops of the hip bones (ilia) down into the knees and lift the spine. Be careful to keep the abdomen and buttocks soft and the energy of the chest dropping.

Once you are in the pose, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, slowly lower your hips on an inhalation and return to the seated position. With Camel Pose, you begin to develop balance and strength in the spine, promoting flexibility in the shoulders and suppleness in the abdomen. By relying less on outer sight for your sense of identity and position in the world, you can cultivate an inner vision that expands into your more authentic, intuitive self.

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

Key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

For FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

Estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.
