#8701. Transform Your Core with This 10-Minute Exercise Ball Workout

An exercise (or stability) ball is an inexpensive but effective strength training tool for triathletes. (Photo: Getty Images)

For this article, retired pro triathlete and Triathlete contributor Emma-Kate Lidbury spoke to strength coach and former pro Dede Griesbauer about why this stability ball workout is so effective for triathletes.

Here’s the thing about strength training for triathletes: Almost nobody skips it because they don’t believe in it. They skip it because of the drive to the gym or the 90 minutes that don’t exist between that threshold bike workout and school pickup.

So what if we make life a little easier and remove some of the barriers to getting strength done?

This routine does exactly that and requires one piece of equipment – an exercise ball – and a patch of floor about the size of a yoga mat. No need for dumbbells, a bench, a gym membership, or the drive there. You can pick up an exercise ball for about the same price as a mid-range pair of goggles; it can fit into most any suitcase; and it might just help you find every stabilizer muscle you’ve quietly neglected since your last off-season strength block.

A stability ball is, by design, unstable. That’s the entire value proposition. It offers the following benefits:

Every exercise here demands you hold a neutral spine against something actively trying to move you out of it. Former pro triathlete turned strength coach Dede Griesbauer points out that this pays off in two places triathletes care about: run efficiency, and the ability to hold a stable position in the aerobars.

With an exercise like the rear foot elevated lunge (below), Griesbauer notes this forces each leg to work independently, which may reveal the left-right discrepancies a bilateral squat lets you hide. This matters for power balance on the bike and for not favoring one side on the run, which can help reduce injury risk.

Almost every movement in this routine trains multiple muscle groups at once. Griesbauer’s summary: It offers good “bang for the buck” with minimal equipment, minimal space, and minimal setup.

Griesbauer advises adding strength work to your hard days, not because it’s pleasant to stack lifting onto a threshold run, but because the alternative – sprinkling it across easy days – erodes the recovery that those days are designed to deliver.

“Make your hard days hard so that your easy days can be easy,” she says.

That’s the ideal. Griesbauer is also clear about what “ideal” might look like for an age-grouper with a job.

“Not everyone will have time to do their hard bike or run session AND make time for strength on the same day,” she says. “The good news is that this session isn’t heavy loading. These are good basic movements, so if you are time-crunched, adding them wherever you can is better than not doing them at all.”

Two sessions a week is the target, but once isn’t a failure. “Some is better than none,” Griesbauer says, “so if you can only do it once? Get it done once.”

Start with a single pass through all nine exercises (which should take approximately 10-12 minutes).

Once one round stops feeling like work, add a second. Then, if time allows, add a third. Three circuits should take you about 30-35 minutes and is plenty of stimulus for a routine that isn’t loading you heavily. Rest 30 to 60 seconds between exercises and a couple of minutes between rounds.

Progress through the workout in the order listed. It moves between lower body, core, and upper body so nothing fatigues to failure.

Stand on your right foot with your left leg extended behind you and the top of your left foot resting on the ball. Bend your right knee until your right thigh is parallel to the floor, keeping your torso upright and your weight on your heel. Now press your heel into the floor and return to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions and then repeat the exercise with your left leg.

Begin in a prone position with the tops of your feet resting on the ball, your palms on the floor underneath your shoulders, and your body forming a straight line. Now contract your stomach muscles, bend your knees, and roll the ball toward your chest. Pause briefly and roll the ball back until your body forms a straight line again. Complete 12 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your feet together, your body forming a perfectly straight line and your palms positioned slightly more than shoulder-width apart on the ball. Bend your elbows and smoothly lower your chest to within an inch of the ball. Immediately press back upward to the start position. If you have difficulty doing a full push-up, do a half push-up, bending your elbows only to 90 degrees before pressing upward. Complete 10 repetitions.

Start in a bridge position, face up, with your head and shoulders on the floor and your heels resting on top of the ball, your body suspended in a straight line between these points. Contract your hamstrings and roll the ball toward your butt. Pause briefly and extend your legs, rolling the ball back to the starting point. Don’t let your hips drop. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, elevating one foot above the ball and pulling the ball toward your butt with the other leg.

Kneel on the floor facing the ball, lean forward slightly, and place your forearms on top of the ball. Pull your belly button toward your spine. Slowly roll the ball forward by extending your forearms out in front of you and allowing your body to tilt toward the floor. Concentrate on maintaining perfect alignment of your spine. Stop just before you’re forced to arch your back. Hold this position for a two-count and then return to the start position, exhaling as you do so. Complete 12 repetitions.

Lie facedown on the ball with your palms on the floor. Begin with the ball supporting your pelvic area. Now use your hands to drag your body forward over the ball until it is underneath the tops of your feet, keeping your body in a straight line. Pause briefly and roll back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your palms on the floor, the tops of your feet resting on the ball, and your body in a perfectly straight line between them. Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor. Go as far as you can without strain; it’s OK if it isn’t very far. Now press back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Lie face up with your upper back supported by the ball, your feet flat on the floor about 12 inches apart, your knees bent and your body forming a “tabletop” from knees to chest. Contract your calf muscles and raise your heels off the floor without allowing your hips to sag. Now lower your heels back to the floor. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, first crossing your left ankle over your right knee and then doing the reverse.

Get into a plank position with your palms on the floor underneath your chest and the ball supporting your shins. Keeping your arms straight, press the heels of your palms into the floor and push your body backward so that the ball rolls up under your thighs. Go as far as you can and then pull your body in the opposite direction until you’re back in the start position. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, start with the ball under the tops of your feet.

Instability is the point, which also means this routine isn’t universally appropriate. Griesbauer flags a few pointers worth knowing before you start. Note that none of these are a reason not to train. They just require you to adapt or swap movements if needed.

If you have a cranky lower back: The abdominal rollout generates high spinal extension and shear force if your core gives out mid-rep, which can be a genuine problem for anyone with disc history. The reverse crunch can pull you into loaded lumbar flexion if control slips, and a hamstring curl performed with dropped hips will arch and cramp the low back.

If you have “shoulder history”: Push-ups on a moving ball tax the rotator cuff hard, and the ball walk-out places prolonged, shifting load on the shoulder joint. Skip both if you’ve dealt with instability or impingement.

If you have wrist issues: The ball’s spherical surface forces the wrists into deep extension while the weight moves under you. Elevated push-ups shift more bodyweight forward onto the same joints.

If you have knees and hip flexor problems: The rear foot elevated lunge loads the front knee in deep flexion and stretches the trailing leg aggressively, which can be enough to tip the pelvis if your hip flexors are tight. Tight hip flexors will also hijack the reverse crunch from the lower abs.

If you have cramp-prone calves and hamstrings: The bridge heel raise fires the calves while the hamstrings are already shortened, which is a reliable spasm trigger. The hamstring curl frequently cramps athletes with weak hamstrings on the concentric.

If you have compromised balance: Any single-leg work raises fall risk. Have a wall or chair within reach if you feel you might need it.

#8700. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Good point Stephanie – I believe that part is coming soon, as the first batch of apartments open up and are ready for rent (right now you are only signing up for the waiting list rather than an actual apartment).

Since I was there and asked the same question in person, the answer is basically “market rate” – in other words, when a new apartment goes up for rent, the builders typically conduct a price survey of what would be a competitive price at that moment, and then they start advertising at that price.

Just like any other supply and demand sensitive thing, these prices will then fluctuate based on the demand level until you lock it in with a lease. During my tour, it was a hot time for rentals in prosperous Tempe so the rent was around $2.50 per square foot per month, or a little under $2k for a large 1-bedroom apartment.

Note that at Culdesac you get a few extra perks included in that rent: internet access that works across the whole 17 acre campus, gym, pool, and unlimited transit pass along with credits for bike and carshare as well.

#8697. Why I Lug My Own Props to Yoga Class

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

I had been practicing yoga for years before I discovered the magic of lugging my own mat to class.

Before that, I’d simply borrowed the cheap but convenient studio mats that were available for use. I considered myself too lazy to grapple with a heavy mat as I hauled it from the car to the studio and back again. But following some serious thought about functionality and germ exposure after I ended up with plantar warts (I mean, think about it), I decided it was worth the trouble to practice on my own sturdy mat.

And it was. I found more stability in standing poses from the mat’s refusal to slide or wrinkle on the floor, benefited from its extra grippiness in twists and backbends, and appreciated its additional cushioning in seated poses. It’s no exaggeration to say practicing on my own mat revolutionized my studio experience.

But I didn’t stop there. Following that experience, I began to look askance at other props in the studio—namely, blankets, bolsters, blocks, and straps—which appeared as broken in (or broken down?) as those loaner mats. And, I suspected, just as germy.

So I started bringing my own props—and my own germs—to class. Well, within reason. No sandbags or headstand bench, obviously. But I did load myself up before each class with the basics, including a blanket, strap, and block. If I was heading to a yin or restorative class, I brought my own bolster, too. I’d find my own comfort and marinate in my own sweat, thank you.

I’ve been doing this for 20 years. Beyond basic hygiene, the benefits of using my own props include functionality. Before you say blocks are blocks and blankets are blankets, they come in a dizzying array of shapes and materials, not to mention designs and colors. Do I want a foam block? Wood? Cork? Recycled materials? Purple? Pink? Black? Would my hands rather settle on a support that is rectangular, circular, oval, or square?

And as for a blanket, am I more of a pressed wool “yoga blanket” person or is a pretty “Mexican blanket” more my style? And don’t get me started on bolsters, with nearly infinite options for shapes and styles.

When I curate my DIY yoga props each class, I’m arming myself with props that I’ve worked with before and that strategically suit my body and take me even further into my practice. And because they are set to my preferences, I know them well enough to put them to effective use in a nanosecond.

My strap, for instance, is knotted in strategic locations, including one that makes it easy for me to reel in an errant back leg in my much-practiced Natarajasana (Dancer Pose). When that stays consistent from class to class, it makes it easier for me to find my version of the posture, which in turn means my focus can remain on the demands of the pose rather than fumbling with a strap or figuring out the height to adjust my block.

And although it’s about so much more than looks, it’s also about the looks. I just like having something pretty and functional and familiar surrounding me during my practice. My black mat, purple knotted strap, cork block, and wildly beautiful purple, orange, and teal bolster fit me to a T.

What matters is that by the time I’ve arranged the props around my mat, I’ve built what looks and feels like a cocoon of comfort. I’m no longer practicing in a gym-like room with a bunch of strangers. Rather, it’s as if I’m in my own private studio with my own private equipment among my own private germs. Yoga feels best when it also feels safe.

#8694. Post-Race Weight Gain: Why You’re Heavier After Finishing a Race (And Why It’s a Good Thing)

You wake up feeling sore and puffy the day after a race, step on the scale, and confirm what you intuitively feel: you’re a few pounds above your pre-race weight.

But why? Logically, a massive calorie burn (up to 10,000+ calories for an Ironman!) should tip the scale the other way, so something must be wrong.

Your first impulse may be to cut calories or jump right back into training. Please don’t! What you’re seeing is your body’s normal physiological response as it goes into full recovery mode.

Post-race weight gain isn’t the same as the off-season weight drift many athletes experience. That weight tends to build over months and is a separate conversation about energy balance. The jump you see on the scale in the first 24 to 72 hours after the race is mostly water. Specifically, your body is hard at work replenishing glycogen, rebuilding plasma volume, and retaining water and sodium as part of its hormonal stress-and-repair response. It’s most noticeable after a half or full iron-distance triathlon, where fueling, fluid intake, and stress load are highest.

Let’s dig into what’s going on, and why this temporary bump is actually a good sign.

Long-course races drain your muscle glycogen. As long as you eat plenty of carbs, your body starts refilling those stores within the first few hours after you finish. But the longer the race, the more muscle damage, which slows the process.

After a long-course race, full restoration can take several days, rather than the roughly 24 hours we see after shorter events. Here’s the kicker: each gram of newly synthesized glycogen is stored with approximately three grams of water. So, replenishing 400–500 grams of muscle glycogen adds about 3.5–4.5 pounds, mostly from water, packed in your muscles. In other words, much of the bump you see on the scale in the first few days is restored fuel.

Glycogen isn’t the only reason the scale climbs. It’s normal to finish a long race dehydrated, since even a solid race hydration strategy can’t fully offset hours of sweat losses. In the 24 to 72 hours after the race, fluid-conserving hormones (aldosterone and vasopressin) remain elevated, signaling your body to hold onto fluid to restore plasma volume and electrolyte balance. The extra water weight won’t stick around long, so don’t cut back on fluids or salt to bring the number down. Your body needs both right now.

Racing 70.3 or 140.6 miles puts your body under more stress than a typical training day. During and after the race, cortisol, your primary stress hormone, spikes, signaling your body to retain water. Prolonged physical exertion causes muscle microdamage and inflammation.

The longer, hotter, and tougher the race, the longer recovery may take. As your body begins repairs, fluid moves into damaged tissues, which can explain your tight, swollen legs. You’ll notice improvement when your kidneys start clearing the excess fluid, leading to more frequent bathroom visits. A little puffiness for a couple of days post-race means the repair process is underway.

As training volume comes down after a race, you might expect your appetite to follow. And, for the first several hours, it often does, since hard effort can temporarily suppress hunger. But over the next day or two, it returns with a vengeance. That’s because a slower-moving hormonal system (primarily ghrelin and leptin) signals your brain to respond to the energy deficit you built up on race day.

You may feel hungrier for several days, often craving energy-dense, salty, carb-rich foods (think fries, burgers, and pizza). And all that yummy food, along with the water and sodium that come with it, adds to the scale number too. It’s not a lack of willpower or a total loss of control; it’s your body refueling.

Following an endurance race, some swelling is expected, but I’d be remiss not to flag a few scenarios that, although rare, require medical attention.

If one leg swells, especially with calf pain, warmth, or redness, it may indicate a blood clot. Swelling with shortness of breath or chest pain is an emergency; seek immediate attention.

Dark cola-colored urine with severe muscle pain or weakness could signal rhabdomyolysis: a condition involving severe muscle breakdown that can lead to kidney damage.

And if you finish the race heavier than you started and experience confusion, headache, or nausea, it could be hyponatremia (low blood sodium); seek medical help right away.

For most athletes, a few extra pounds in the days after a long-distance race signals a healthy recovery. Still, it can be tempting, especially if you keep close tabs on your weight, to see the number go up and immediately want to cut back or restrict.

Resist the urge. Your body needs carbohydrates and protein to rebuild glycogen and repair tissue; your fluid and electrolyte balance needs restoring, and your immune system needs adequate energy while under duress. Restricting food and fluids now won’t get your weight back on track. It will delay glycogen restoration, prolong fatigue and soreness, and potentially increase your risk of illness.

As your fluid levels normalize and inflammation subsides, most of the extra weight comes off naturally, typically within three to seven days. You’ve demanded a lot from your body in training and on race day, so give it what it needs: plenty of nutrient-rich food, adequate hydration, rest, and quality sleep. Then step back and trust your body and the process.

#8692. 8 Simple Yin Yoga Poses to Release Tension From Your Entire Body

This yin yoga for a full-body stretch routine includes relatively simple shapes with options that help you find your comfort level, even if you’re new to yin yoga. In this style of stretching, we hold shapes for an extended period of time, but we don’t use any kind of muscular effort. Yin yoga is not about getting stronger and it’s not about endurance. It’s about relaxing in all of the poses and letting gravity do the work for you to send the stretch into the joints as well as the connective tissues.

You’re always trying to find your edge in these poses, which means you’re not trying to be so intense that you need to tense your body or hold your breath. You should experience some sensation, but it should never ever feel painful. Especially because you want to be able to stay in each stretch for several minutes. Usually a yin yoga pose is held for three to five minutes, although if you’re a beginner, then start by staying for a little less time, because even two minutes can feel like an eternity!

Basically, yin yoga is meant to consist of simple shapes held for a little longer than usual, and you’ll definitely feel the difference by the end of it. Think of this as an introduction to yin yoga and know that there are so many more poses to explore.

You definitely don’t need props to practice yin yoga. But it can be helpful to know how to use them to experience more support in the poses, so for the following poses, I suggest you consider using props, whether two blocks and a strap or, if you don’t have those at home, you can use some pillows or couch cushions and a belt or even a sweatshirt. There are all sorts of everyday household items you can use in place of props.

Kneel on the mat, bring your big toes together, and then let your knees go apart. The wider your knees, the more intense the stretch through the inner thighs. You don’t want to cause any kind of pinching or compression in your lower back. If you feel tightness or tension there, it usually means your knees are too far apart and you simply need to bring them slightly closer together.

Walk your hands away from you and lean your chest toward the mat. You can either rest your forehead on the mat or stack your hands and use them or a pillow as support for your forehead in Child’s Pose. You can also bring a block or firm pillow lengthwise under your chest and forehead to close any gap between your body and the mat and then rest your body on that while turning your head to one side.

Try to let your hips be heavy as they sink toward your heels. Let your chest melt toward the mat or the support beneath you. Relax your arms and shoulders and upper back, and simply breathe slow and steady, in and out through your nose. Stay here for about 2 minutes.

When you’re ready to come out of the pose, bring your palms to the mat and press into them so you can start to lift your head and chest back up.

Slide forward onto your belly with your legs straight behind you. Try to keep your feet about hip-distance apart. Then bring your forearms in front of you with your elbows a little in front of your shoulders and your palms about shoulder-distance apart in Sphinx Pose.

You get to control how intense you make this backbend. The farther forward you bring your forearms, the easier the stretch across the front of your back and the less compression in your lower back. Alternatively, you can make the stretch a little more intense by bringing your elbows directly underneath your shoulders.

Now press your shoulders back a little, so you’re lightly squeezing your shoulder blades behind you. Keep your chin parallel to the floor and think about gently reaching your chest forward. If there’s pinching or compression or any kind of pain in your lower back, you know you’ve gone a little too far in the pose and you want to bring your arms a little more forward to lessen the backbend.

Feel your rib cage expand front to back and side to side with the rhythm of your breath. Stay here for about 2 minutes.

Very slowly release out of the pose and lower your chest back down to the mat.

Come to your hands and knees and you might want to keep your blocks within reach for this one. Step your right foot forward in between your palms in Low Lunge. I like to fold the left edge of the mat onto itself underneath my left knee to pad it since we’ll be here for a little while. You can also slide a folded blanket or pillow underneath your back knee.

Try to keep your right ankle underneath your right knee as you keep your hands on the mat or bring blocks underneath your palms. Then let your hips sink forward and down. Release the shoulders away from your ears and let gravity do the work for you here in this hip-opening stretch.

If you need to take any breaks, you’re welcome to straighten your front leg and release it. Otherwise, try to let yourself ease into the pose.

When you’re ready to come out of the pose, start to push down into your right heel to slowly lift yourself and bring yourself back to hands and knees. Before we repeat the same pose on the other side, it might feel good to do a few hip circles or take another brief Child’s Pose. Just notice the difference in how you feel from one side to the other.

This time, step your left foot forward in between your hands at the top of the mat and keep your hands to either side of that front foot while keeping your chest lifted. Try not to collapse your weight into your wrists. Keep pressing into the fingertips and knuckles.

When you’re ready to come out, come to a seat on the mat.

This is basically a seated forward fold. You’ll probably want to have your blocks handy for this one. Just extend your legs straight in front of you. You want your feet to be about hip-distance apart. Then lean forward in a Seated Forward Bend known as Caterpillar. In yin yoga, when you bend forward, you’re not pushing or pulling or forcing your way into a more intense stretch. In fact, you want to just let you back round and the rest of your body relax into the pose with very little effort. I like to turn my palms to face upward so I’m not tempted to push or pull my way deeper into the pose.

Your legs do not need to be perfectly straight. You can absolutely bend your knees if that’s more comfortable for you. Let yourself relax into the pose, including your neck. If your chest is somewhere close to the mat, you might want to prop yourself up with a block either under your chest or forehead. If your chest is a little more upright, you can use both blocks stacked beneath you so you have some support.

You might feel the stretch along the entire back of the body, from the head down the spine and all the way into the back of the legs to the heels. The longer you stay in this pose, the more you might notice that your body might slip a little deeper into the stretch. The pose tends to change quite a little the longer we hold it. Simply stay here and see what happens.

When you’re ready to lift yourself out of the pose, go extra slowly since forward folds can be quite intense for the low back. Start by flipping your palms, pushing your hands into the mat, and using arm strength to lift yourself, inch by inch. You’re really not rushing this. Keep breathing evenly as you transition out of the poses.

Keep your left leg straight in front of you and bend your right knee. Bring your right foot across your body and rest it on the mat to the outside of your left thigh. Grab your right knee with your left hand and start to turn your chest toward the right, bringing your right fingertips behind your right hip, and continue to twist toward the right as you squeeze your right thigh toward your belly.

Try to eliminate any rounding in your spine. Think instead of grounding into the mat and, at the same time, reaching the crown of the head toward the ceiling while releasing your shoulders down and away from your ears. So you want to be lengthening through the spine a little more each time you inhale. Maybe you close your eyes, paying attention to your breath in and out through your nose.

When you’re ready to release, slowly unwind and face forward. Then switch sides, extending your right leg straight in front of you, bending your left knee and crossing your left foot over your right thigh. And then twist and rotate the spine from there, hugging the belly toward the spine.

When you’re ready, unwrap and face forward again.

Grab your strap and lower all the way down onto your back. Bend your knees and bring your feet flat on the mat about hip-distance apart. Bring your right knee toward your chest and drape the strap around the ball of your right foot. Then extend your right leg straight toward the ceiling.

My favorite way to do this reclined hamstring stretch is instead of actively reaching my arms to hold the strap, I let my upper arms relax against the mat. Then I don’t need to use quite as much arm strength.

Let your right leg be soft and relaxed, using just a little arm strength to guide the leg toward your chest. Just like in your seated forward fold, you can absolutely bend your right knee. If you’d like to make this stretch a little more sensational, slide your left leg straight on the mat. Sometimes the lifted leg will shake a little, and that’s usually just a sign that you’re taking the pose a little too far.

To come out of the pose, bend your right knee and remove the strap. Then switch sides. Wrap the strap around your left foot, extend your left leg straight up, and find your stretch.

When you’re ready, slowly release the strap and remain lying on your back.

So our next pose is one of my all-time favorite yin yoga poses. It’s called Banana Pose for reasons you’ll understand shortly. It’s a great way to open the sides of your body.

Stay on your back and shimmy your hips as far over toward the right of the mat as you can. Then bring your shoulders and your chest a little more toward the left. Extend your legs straight, and then inch your ankles toward the left in a banana shape.

You can reach your arms overhead and rest them wherever is comfortable or bend your elbows and hold onto opposite forearms. Try to keep your right hip grounded to the floor as much as possible.

If you want a slightly more intense stretch, cross your right ankle over your left ankle. You will probably feel a nice opening along the waist, hip, and along the IT band along your outer thigh. Sometimes it takes a little readjusting until you can find the sweet spot where it’s not too intense and not too hard to hold. You want it to be comfortable enough that you could stay here for a few minutes without having to readjust.

Try to send your breath to the right side of your body, filling up the space you’re creating, and relaxing into the pose a little more with every exhalation.

If you had your ankles crossed, you can let that go. Then we’re going to ease into the stretch on the other side, shifting your hips over to the left side of the mat  while the upper body moves to the right, and then reaching with your upper body as well.

You might want your blocks for this one. Still lying on your back, bring the soles of your feet together to touch. Make sure your shoulders and your hips are in line, and let your knees open wide. If the lower back or the hips feel really tight, you can use your blocks beneath your knees or thighs so there’s a little support here, which will make the pose easier. Otherwise, you can just let your legs fall open and let your arms rest wherever is comfortable. You can even reach your arms alongside your head if you want to stretch the shoulders and upper back. Send your breath all the way down to your low belly and low back.

When you’re ready to come out of the pose, you can use your hands to help your knees come back together or you can settle straight into the next pose.

In this last pose, straighten your legs in front of you and slightly out to the sides, and let your body take up space. Rest your arms somewhere comfortable, palms facing upward, and just let yourself release into the shape. Maybe you quietly notice the effects of your practice on your body, your mind, and your breath. Release any tension in your facial muscles and your jaw and simply let yourself be.

When you’re ready, begin to lengthen your breath as you slowly wake back up. Maybe you wiggle your fingers and toes or circle your wrists and ankles. Let your head slowly turn from side to side. Then take a stretch by extending your arms overhead. Eventually, you can slowly sit up nice and tall, closing your eyes. Bring your hands together at the front of the chest and simply notice what feels differently. Thank you for doing this beginner yin yoga for a full-body stretch with me. I hope you enjoyed it. Let me know what you think in a comment below.

#8689. The Science of “Extreme” Exercise During Pregnancy

The author attended the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto to hear directly from Margie Davenport and Michelle Mottola, key researchers shaping the upcoming 2027 International Olympic Committee guidelines. The resulting piece analyzes their latest clinical and survey data on pregnant athletes engaging in heavy weightlifting, high-intensity intervals, endurance sports, and rock climbing.

Back in 2019, I wrote about a new set of guidelines for exercise during pregnancy. These guidelines were revolutionary—up to a point. Advice from doctors at the time was often extremely conservative, like never letting your heart rate exceed 140 beats per minute. But solid evidence now suggested that consistent moderate exercise—at least 150 minutes spread over at least three days per week—was not just safe for most pregnant women but was actually beneficial for both mother and fetus, dramatically lowering the risk of conditions such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and depression.

Sign up for a ten-part email series from Alex Hutchinson on how to train, fuel, and recover. Each week, Alex covers a new topic, including strength training, supplements, and more!

Beyond that threshold, though, the deadlines dared not tread. Moderate exercise? Sure. Lifting heavy weights, or running marathons, or going rock climbing? That’s a trickier question, because no scientist wants to send a pregnant person out to do something that could potentially harm her or her baby. But ignoring it doesn’t make sense, because many female athletes do continue participating in their sports while pregnant, regardless of what the guidelines say. And those who stop or dramatically reduce their activity may suffer declines in both physical and mental health.

It’s important, then, to understand what the evidence says about the risks and benefits of more extreme forms of exercise. In 2018, the answer was “not much.” But in the years since then, there has been a steady flow of research on pregnant athletes doing hard things. In fact, the International Olympic Committee is planning to release a new and dramatically revised set of guidelines for pregnant athletes in 2027.

At the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto last week, I had a chance to hear two key authors of both the old and new guidelines—Margie Davenport of the University of Alberta and Michelle Mottola of Western University—speak about their research. They couldn’t yet reveal what’s in the new guidelines, but they did share some of the key research that informs them. Here are some highlights from the extreme frontiers of exercise and pregnancy.

Any sort of heavy lifting is frowned upon during pregnancy, and particularly lifting while lying on your back, which could compress key blood vessels. But this advice, Davenport points out, is based on expert opinion and workplace studies, where heavy lifting is different from lifting in the gym where you control load and recovery.

To start, she and her colleagues surveyed 679 recreational weightlifters and CrossFit athletes who were pregnant and habitually lifted at least 80 percent of their one-rep max. Those who continued heavy lifting had a 51 percent reduction in complications compared to those who obeyed the guidelines and dialed back their training. They were also roughly half as likely as normal to report postpartum depression after delivery.

Of course, survey studies have limitations: maybe complications caused people to stop lifting rather than the other way around, for example. But those initial positive results paved the way for bringing 10 pregnant women into the lab and having them do squats, bench press, and deadlift for 10 reps at up to 90 percent of 10-rep max. They monitored maternal and fetal heart rate, umbilical blood pressure, glucose and lactate levels, and various other health markers, and compared the results to those of ten non-pregnant controls; there were no causes for concern.

A heart-rate limit of 140 is outdated. Still, the 2019 guidelines remain cautious. “Vigorous” exercise, they suggest, should top out at around 169 beats per minute for women 29 and younger, and 162 beats per minute for those 30 and older.

In a 2023 study, Davenport and her colleagues put that ceiling to the test. They had 15 volunteers, at an average of 27 weeks pregnant, do either a 30-minute moderate bike ride or 10 x 1:00 intervals at above 90 percent of their predicted maximum heart rate. The women ended up reaching a peak of 96 percent on average during the intervals, with some getting as high as 105 percent of max. (This isn’t Spinal Tap: the standard estimate of max heart rate, 220 minus age, was clearly off for these women.)

Once again, the researchers took a bunch of measures of fetal and maternal physiological responses. There were no relevant differences between the moderate and intense exercise sessions.

This was another survey study: 331 women who, on average, were 33.2 years old and had completed 2.1 pregnancies. All had engaged in exercise bouts lasting at least an hour during their pregnancies; 80 percent had continued long-duration exercise throughout their pregnancies, but in most cases had gradually decreased overall training as the pregnancy progressed.

Davenport and her colleagues divided the respondents into two subgroups: those who continued to do at least 300 minutes of exercise per week during their third trimester, and those who were below that threshold. Those in the high exercise group had a lower risk of complications during delivery, but a higher risk of diastasis recti—a separation of the stomach muscles—after delivery.

The overall conclusion was that long-duration exercise well above guideline recommendations “appears to be well tolerated” by people who are already used to that level of training.

Here’s where things get interesting, because it’s hard to wave away the hypothetical dangers of a hard fall. But do these risks justify telling people not to climb?

Davenport has led a couple of studies exploring this issue. One involved interviewing 11 elite climbers who continued to train or compete during pregnancy about their perspectives on risk. Climbing, one of the climbers said, was actually safer than walking down the street: “I’m less likely to fall because I’ve got three points of contact on, compared to one when I’m walking… So I feel like I’m more likely to trip over something in the dark on the street than falling while climbing up a climbing wall.”

The second study surveyed nearly 700 climbers who had climbed through pregnancy, logging a cumulative total of 64,000 hours of climbing and suffering 155 self-diagnosed “hard falls.” Here there were two adverse events (one vaginal bleeding, the other undeclared), but both births were healthy. Climbing isn’t without risks, Davenport says, but the findings suggest the risks are lower than previously thought. Of note, 96 percent of respondents were “happy” or “very happy” they had continued to climb.

There’s more—Davenport has also studied contact sports like soccer, for example—but you get the picture. Some of these activities clearly involve theoretical risks, but those theoretical risks need to be balanced against the measurable mental and physical benefits of continuing to train and the risks of stopping. One of the best predictors of post-pregnancy injury, for example, is having reduced your training by more than 50 percent during pregnancy.

The focus of the upcoming IOC guidelines will be “athlete-centered decision-making”—not an ironclad set of rules about who can do which types of exercise when, but a framework about how to weigh the pros and cons in different contexts. It’s an important update, because it recognizes what’s already happening in the real world. “Our current public health guidance is fantastic and sets our baseline,” Davenport says. “But most athletes—well, all athletes—are going to vastly exceed current recommendations.”

For more Sweat Science, sign up for the email newsletter and check out my new book The Explorer’s Gene: Why We Seek Big Challenges, New Flavors, and the Blank Spots on the Map.

#8687. If You Don’t Practice Yoga in the Morning, You Might Be Missing Out. Here’s What Science Says.

When I first started practicing online yoga to address the tightness and discomfort I was experiencing from sitting all day, I snuck yoga into my schedule literally whenever I could. Noon. After work. Before bed.

But the more I scrolled for practices, the more I noticed one theme showing up again and again. Namely, morning yoga. Curious, I searched YouTube for “morning yoga” and found literally thousands of videos. Yoga with Kassandra has an entire Morning Yoga playlist featuring more than 238 videos, some of which have drawn more than two million views each. Yoga With Adriene has a “Morning Mobility Yoga” video from a couple years ago that was just shy of 10 million views. That got me wondering whether there are more benefits of morning yoga as opposed to practicing it at other times of day. Being a night owl, I found that I was most likely to unroll my mat in the evenings. Should I change my habits?!

Turns out, the answer is complicated. There are definite benefits of morning yoga, yet a lot depends on why you’re practicing yoga as well as your personal quirks.

There’s been a surprising amount of scientific research on the benefits of morning yoga. And let’s not overlook the fact that, historically, many yoga traditions favored practicing yoga in the early morning. I mean, take Sun Salutations, which is a sequence of poses, or asana, performed facing east as the sun peeps over the horizon. And depending on your schedule and your personality, there can also be practical reasons.

There’s a very real possibility of becoming so distracted or delayed by work or life that practicing yoga doesn’t happen at all if it doesn’t happen in the morning. Just ask anyone who’s ever intended to make a late-afternoon studio class but ended up stuck at work or feeling too defeated by the day to crawl onto their mat.

Yet the evidence for this anecdotal experience is limited. Research on exercise adherence is inconclusive in terms of whether morning or evening is better, with some research suggesting that practicing at a consistent time of day is more relevant than the exact time of day. But if you do unroll your mat in the morning, even if your day falls off the rails, at least you gave yourself yoga beforehand.

If you can find time to make it onto your mat later in the day, one study suggests mental distraction is more of an issue during evening practices. Whether the distractions take the shape of ruminating over the day or contemplating the things that still need to be accomplished before night’s end, it’s possible you will encounter fewer distractions in the mornings.

And although bringing yourself back to a quiet mind is the purpose of yoga, perhaps you don’t need any additional challenges in that realm.

One study suggests that daily morning yoga supported “emotional well-being” more than less frequent evening yoga participation. This was tested across two groups: one that attended Ashtanga yoga classes at 7 am for two work weeks; the second practiced Ashtanga yoga at night once or twice from Monday to Friday for two weeks. Though both groups had practiced in the evening previously, the morning group experienced greater change after the two-week study.

Of course, the increased frequency of practicing five times a week might have also affected the participants. More yoga is usually better than less.

A recent 2026 study on morning versus evening online yoga found that practicing early in the day (6 to 7 am) was better than evening yoga (6 to 7 pm) in terms of effects on sleep and lifestyle in a group of young adults. Specifically, they found that morning yoga improved energy and restfulness. It also enhanced participants’ self-reported psychological health over the course of the four-week study.

An earlier study also found that practicing morning yoga can help minimize morning sleepiness.

If you’re someone who likes your yoga vigorous, stick with morning sessions. A 2024 review of multiple studies found that, overall, more intense activity, including yoga, at night could easily disrupt sleep. Morning sessions didn’t have the same effect.

Research is somewhat limited on the topic of morning yoga reducing stress. Yet a 2023 study compared morning yoga and gym practices (6 to 9 am) against evening yoga and gym practices (6 to 10 pm). The morning yoga group experienced lower cortisol than the morning gym workout group. The researchers theorized this supports feeling happier, more optimistic, and being able to pay attention and work with more efficiency throughout the day.”

As with much in life, there is no one-size-fits-all answer regarding when to practice yoga. The best yoga for you is the yoga that you’re actually going to do, whatever the time of day, style, intensity, and length. Although if you’re looking for a reason to make time to unroll your mat in the a.m., there are more than enough reasons to try it. Chances are, it won’t take long to experience the benefits yourself.

#8685. Frugal Man Buys $52,000 Car – Why??

As I type this, I’m jumping through the various hoops involved in buying a 2023 Tesla Model Y, a rather expensive, luxury “crossover” that is absolutely loaded to the gills with excess: all wheel drive, faster acceleration than a Lamborghini, enough space for seven people and enough computer gadgetry to function as a small Google data center.

Update: Looking for the ongoing tracker page? It’s here at “The Model Y Experiment“

The total net cost of this thing to me after all the taxes and tax credits* will be about $52,000, which is just a stunning amount higher than the Honda van it is replacing. That old classic cost me $4500 when I bought it off of Craigslist twelve years ago, and it had served me dutifully until just last month, crisscrossing the mountains and deserts of this country and also helping to rebuild a considerable swath of houses in my neighborhood.

I’m supposed to be a frugality-oriented financial blogger, and I’m also known for hating car culture – I think most people use cars about ten times more often than they need to, and most people drive cars they can’t afford. So why the hell am I buying a new one?

From those first three paragraphs, you can see I’m feeling plenty of self-mockery and ridicule over this new purchase. If you’re also a naturally frugal person, you can surely relate to the thoughts and you probably also agree with me that I’m off my rocker.

And indeed, I’m still on-board with frugality and healthy self mockery. After all, it was this overall life philosophy that earned me an early retirement 18 years ago, which provides all of the glorious freedom I enjoy now.

It was also the philosophy that allowed me to procrastinate on buying this expensive car for the last four years, even as countless people both close to me and out on the Internet egged me on and told me I should just loosen up and treat myself.

But there’s a classic slogan that applies to many areas of life, and it is something I like to dig up and ponder every now and then:

How does that piece of wisdom apply to frugal living and enjoying a long life of early retirement?

A quick story from a recent run to the grocery store will explain:

I was standing there in the bakery aisle, hoping to restock with a loaf of Dave’s Killer Bread for the next day’s breakfast with some visiting friends. But since this was in a standard grocery store rather than the Costco where I usually shop, the damned stuff was priced at an eye-watering $6.99 per loaf (instead the $4.50 or so I’m accustomed to paying, and even at the bulk store this stuff is about double the price of normal bread).

“WHO THE HELL DO YOU THINK YOU ARE, TRYING TO SELL BREAD FOR SEVEN BUCKS!!!”

Then I went through a whole mental battle of what I call Grocery Shopping With Your Middle Finger:

“Hmm I wonder if any of the other competing brands are any good?”

“What else is a good substitute for bread for this breakfast?”

And then thankfully, after exhausting all other mental options, I settled on the correct one:

“Because you are never going to wake up in the future and look at your bank account and think, shit, if only I had an extra $2.49 in there I would be a happier person.”

That night, I came home from the store and shared this funny tale with one of my guests. He understood perfectly because he too had earned his own retirement through a lifetime of grinding in tough jobs and disciplined frugality. And despite the fact that he has a net worth several times higher than mine, he admitted that he faces exactly the same mental battles over splurging on himself.

This same friend gives freely to charitable causes, has supported a local school for decades, and is always the first one to pull out the checkbook if a friend has hit hard times or is looking for a trusted business investor.

But he still has trouble bringing himself to take an Uber to the airport instead of riding the bus which takes an hour longer.

We both realized that we were being too cheap with ourselves, and we needed to work on it. And we came up with a set of three ideas that should hopefully work together to help us have more fun with our life savings, while we are still alive:

Principle #1: The Minimum Spending Budget:

Suppose you’ve done well over the years and amassed a pile of productive investments worth about two million dollars. Yes, this is a lot of money for most people, and that is the point: this hypothetical person truly has it made.

But as it turns out, most Mustachians I know with this level of wealth are still living very efficient lives, usually with a spending level of under $40,000 per year. On top of that, they typically live in a mortgage-free house and still have various forms of side income from a small business or two.

The 4% rule tells us that this person should be fairly safe spending up to about $80,000 per year from that cozy nest egg, even if they never earn any other money.

If this person wanted to be ridiculously conservative and set the spending rate at 3%, that still leaves about $60,000 of fun money every single year.. Plus, again, any side income, future inheritances, and social security income only add to the surplus.

Thus, a reasonable minimum spending level for this person might be $60,000 per year.

And in most cases, they know this, but still go right on living on $40k or less and claim they have everything they could ever want.

But if you watch carefully you’ll still catch them firing up the middle finger at things like $6.99 Dave’s bread or the $14.00 Cabernet at the restaurant or driving around in a gas guzzler even when they would prefer to have a proper, modern electric car.

And whenever these people do get extra money, their first instinct is to stash it away on top of the already-too-big pile.  In diagram form, their money flow looks like this:

Note that while this person is great at accumulating money through that big red arrow firing money back into the ‘stash, their “fun stuff” arrow appears quite flaccid and withered.

Principle #2 – the Dedicated Money Wasting Account

Lifelong habits are hard to break, and it’s sometimes hard to “waste” your own hard-earned money on things that seem frivolous, even when you know intellectually that you have way more money than you’ll ever spend.

But have you ever noticed that if you are spending somebody else’s money, preferably an anonymous corporation, it feels different?

For example, when you’re on a business trip and you just show up at the dining table to eat and drink and you never see the bill, you probably don’t fret about the prices, right?

The key is to make your own money feel like somebody else’s, and you can do it like this:

Principle #3 – The Splurge Accountability Buddy

Many of us frugal people tend to stick together. And most of us have different versions of the same problem: we know logically that money is plentiful these days, but our emotions keep us stuck in our old ways of optimizing too much.

But I find that when I team up with local friends who are actually trying to battle these same habits, we can question each other’s decisions, call out cheapness when we see it, and cheer on splurges when we know the other guy would enjoy it.

My super wealthy friend from above has become much better about treating himself (and his family) to quality goods for the home, amazing trips together, and just a general reduction in his stress over being “efficient with money”

My friend and HQ co-owner Carl (Mr. 1500 Days) has finally replaced his beaten-down minivan with a spiffy new Chevrolet Bolt electric car, and is loving that leap into the future.

And of course Mr. Money Mustache, after squeezing one final mountain road trip out of his 23-year-old Honda van, is finally allowing himself to get the Tesla he has been talking about for half a decade.

A recent life change (becoming a co-owner of a fixer-upper vacation rental compound in beautiful Salida Colorado) has reignited the travel fire in my heart and made me realize how much I do love getting out to distant places for visiting, mountain biking, gathering with groups of friends and my favorite activity of all: Carpentourism.

Running the Numbers: how ridiculously expensive is this car?

This is the perfect start to my experiment in spending more. Realistically, a $50,000 car is going to cost me about $10,000 more per year than my old van was burning.  With the biggest costs being these:

Since I personally had a spending deficit of several times more than $10k per year, I figure this is a solid first step. And, since the car’s primary purpose is things like epic camping trips, dream dates, and  long adventures around the country, it will definitely help me spend more on experiences, hotels, and go out to dinner a bit more often as well.

“This Privileged Rich Folk Talk is Making Me Sick, why don’t you give your money away to charity, or to me?”

In general, I agree: the world has problems and the richer you are, the more you should consider giving generously.

But also, to be honest, the whiny people who constantly send complaints like this out to strangers on the Internet really need to get a life. It’s great to encourage philanthropy through positive examples, but completely unproductive to send negativity to shame people you don’t even know for not following your own personal value system. The world has seen more than enough of this.

On top of that, this one-sided thinking can be counterproductive. Both of my friends have given generously throughout their lifetimes. In my own case, I have donated over $500,000 to the best causes I could find during the years I’ve been writing this blog, but I was still refusing to let myself replace that 23-year-old van.

And that overthinking was leading to even more of a scarcity mentality, as I compared my own meager spending to these bigger numbers of my donations, and found myself thinking things like,

“Damn, I’m spending $100 on this dinner date which sounds like a lot, but I also spent ONE THOUSAND TIMES more on donations last year, which sounds like even more. Maybe I am spending too much and need to cut back on EVERYTHING!”And then the fear side of my brain would illogically chime in: “Yeah and you’re going to make us run out of money and be poor forever! waaaah waaaah! Cut back and optimize and conserve!”

Yes – be a super, duper responsible steward of your life savings.

And yes, give generously with all your heart to charity.

But yes, it’s also okay to set aside a portion of the money you’ve earned, for frivolous spending on yourself and those closest to you. You’re not a bad person for having a few nice things.

It’s okay to pay that extra hundred bucks to sit a bit closer to the front of the airplane instead of the back if it helps you enjoy your vacation and spend a joyful half hour walking FREE at your destination while the 49 rows of people behind you fuss infuriatingly with their shit in the overhead bins.

It’s okay to buy the frozen berries at Whole Foods even though they cost eight times more than Costco charges, if it spares you from making a second unpleasant trip through parking lot hell.

And as for me, I am calling it okay to, at last, double flip the Autopilot stalk in my new Tesla and lean back as it it shoots me gracefully through even the highest mountain passes, forever leaving the desperately underpowered wheezing and gear shifting and noise* of the gasoline era behind, forever.

I ended up using an online car salvage service called Peddle*, at the recommendation of a friend. With about five minutes of entering the details of my old Honda, their system offered me $715, and then a towtruck came and took it the next day – and actually gave me the payment in cash, which I found kind of fun. I made a point of using all of that money for splurges like dinners out, in keeping with the theme of this article.

* I later signed this blog up for Peddle’s affiliate program so that link will benefit MMM if you use it.

* A useful tip for more effective splurging:Try to find the truly negative aspects of your life and focus any additional spending on improving those things. But it’s a subtle art so you have to get it right if you want lasting results in happiness.

You don’t want to just reduce hardship or challenge like hiring someone to take care of every aspect of your house, because overcoming daily hardships and having significant accomplishments provides the very core of our life satisfaction.

You also don’t want to just upgrade the things that are already good in your life. For example, a friend of mine is a gourmet coffee expert, and he suggested that I upgrade my setup at home to include on-the-spot roasting, and fancy grinding and brewing equipment. But I already love the good quality coffee I buy off the shelf from Costco, so it would be counterproductive to invest time or money into changing this part of my life.

But when you have something that causes you regular angst and stress, whether it’s a leaky roof that makes you dread rain, or a long commute that makes you dread the daily traffic jam, or a body that is giving you trouble due to not being in the best of shape – those types of things are probably a good target for improvement.

In the case of my car situation, I had a Nissan Leaf which is wonderful to drive, but doesn’t have the range to travel anywhere outside of the Denver metro area. Then I had the van which is a clunky beast to drive, but is otherwise an amazing road tripper because I could bring along whatever and whoever I wanted. But the van was getting increasingly unreliable in several hard-to-fix ways which was making me nervous every time I thought about long distance travel. Which was causing me to avoid certain trips and miss positive lifetime experiences.

In other words, my lack of a reliable long-range car was a small but consistent source of negative stress.

Finally, Vanna gave me the gift of a final hot and smelly transmission failure on a mountain pass on the way home from my new project in Salida. It was just the nudge that I needed. And now I already feel excitement rather than dread at the prospect of all the road trips in the coming decades!

Ok, onto the Tesla. We all know you and many others have been very taken by the oversized electric golf carts. I went and drove a bunch of them myself in an effort to first find something I liked and then do the due diligence to justify a purchase. Do I sound like an engineer? Understandable with all the money I spent becoming one. In the end, I drove just about every EV, so I know the plusses and minuses of many of them. I will say that completely outside of the type of car, Elon has the absolute best way to buy a car. Go online, pick what you want, put in your deposit and wait till it’s ready. No listening to “What can I do to get you in a car today?” from some punk kid at a dealership. But in the end, I had to rely on math. What would it cost for ME to drive an EV of my choice. Well, I’d have to modify that to say the most efficient EV because to me the Audi e Tron GT was levels above every other EV I drove in luxury, quality and feeling more like a car with an electric drive system than an electric motor in tupperware. So the catch for me is that I live in a high electric rate area with wonderful total cost per kWh of 45.5 cents. And I’m seeing gas at the cheapo, competing gas stations for $2.89 per gallon on my way to the used tool store. My daily driver is a 2019 Subaru Crosstrek manual that gets 35 mpg in the summer. Note that ICE cars do worse in the winter because we have “winter gas” but also EVs do even more worse in winter temperatures. So in the end, a Tesla Model 3 single motor (the most efficient EV on the planet) calculates out to cost about 2 cents a mile MORE than my pedestrian Subaru that I bought new for $22k. So unless I’m looking to look like Richie Rich with a new Audi Electromobile, I can’t justify the thought of going electric. I’ll back up a second and admit that you people in like Texas who get electricity for 4 cents a kWh should absolutely look at EVs. But I don’t have that luxury. And gas is cheap here. And I like my car quite a lot with it’s utility, all wheel drive so I don’t have to trump up my driveway in the snow (it’s a steep hill that no 2 wheel drive can get up in snow) and I get fun from rowing gears. So my recommendation for anyone considering an EV is to DO THE MATH. the end.

Haha, yes I remember doing the same math when I saw that article! Although it looks like the Guardian has corrected the numbers in their article so it’s at least a bit less misleading.

It used to say that tires could emit over 9 grams of rubber dust per km of driving, and I calculated at the time the real number is 0.033 grams (33 milligrams) – because a tire loses about 2kg of mass over its 60,000 km lifespan. So, they were off by a factor of almost 300.

Now, they have fixed that to use a figure of 50 milligrams, which is close enough.

I don’t know how to calculate the amount that ends up in the air versus on the road, but either way, you have the same problem with electric cars or gas cars, and nowadays the weight is pretty similar across vehicle classes.

Then, there’s the fact that EVs almost never need their friction brakes, so brake dust is eliminated. And they don’t burn gas or oil, which results in cleaner air. And they are now about to ship in semi truck form, which will eliminate our biggest source of diesel soot. I often come back to the slogan “Everything is a Spectrum” – if you just label things as good or bad as the social media outrage world is prone to do, you miss out on the ability to make nuanced choices and really to make any progress on improving the world.

The best we can do is to make rough estimates of the NUMBERS behind each of our options, and then do tests and collect data so we can refine these numbers over time.

Based on what I’ve read about happiness, humans are generally terrible about figuring out what will make us happy. However, we’re actually very good at identifying things that are making us unhappy; also, unhappiness vs happiness is not a 1:1 comparison (more like 5:1, I believe).

Therefore, eliminating those things that make us unhappy is a logical, sensible and efficient strategy.

For many of us, jobs are the number one cause of dramatic unhappiness, because of the opportunity cost (i.e. time we could be spending on other things we value more), but also stress, commuting, and lack of freedom over our own destiny, etc. So FIRE is the first priority, because that has, by far, the most impact on happiness for most of us. (It’s not the only consideration though, because it takes years to achieve, so the journey matters a lot too).

Once that is achieved, the next steps are going to look very different for everyone, because everyone is different. Many for someone, that’s cutting their own lawn, so they hire someone. For someone else, they hate baking bread, so they buy it pre-made.

Around my house, we refer to it as, “throwing money at the problem”. I detest working on cars, so I always take them to our trusted mechanic. However, I like (or at least don’t mind) carpentry, plumbing, electrical, etc, so I do almost all of that work myself.

MMM identified something that was negatively impacting his level of happiness/life satisfaction, determined the cost to fix it (vs doing other things with that money, because everything is balancing cost/benefit), and decided that the tradeoffs were worth it. It was a decision he researched thoroughly, and although it might not be perfectly logical (although it’s entirely possible it is), he even understood the emotional factors contributing to the decision – we’re humans, not Vulcans! It didn’t impact his life in a negative way financially or otherwise, it doesn’t disproportionately hurt the earth (given the society he lives in), and most importantly, he didn’t make the consumerist mistake of believing that buying the Tesla would make him happy.

That’s the root of the problem for most people, I think – they are constantly fed advertising that convinces them that spending money on something will make them happy. It won’t EVER do that, but using it to remove frustration and pain from your life can definitely improve our level of happiness.

What is optimal consumption though? I think if we are honest, most of us talk a big game about being responsible consumers of resources, but really what is the distinction between justifiable and unjustifiable consumption? Everything up to our own desired level of consumption, we will find a way to say it is justified, and everyone that consumes more resources than us is being frivolous. Not really the basis for a consistent philosophical argument.

On the pure finances side, the point of FIRE in your example is the RE part: Your strategy of going straight to the high-spending model means that you have to work considerably longer, even though you are able to have the luxury spending level for slightly longer. This is still potentially a reason to FIRE even if you don’t care at all about resource consumption.

MMM does his thing very well, which is living like a middle-class guy at a working-class level expenditure, backed by large amounts of financial reserves and a good skillset in case something goes horribly wrong. Somewhere like ERE is more focused on the philosophical examination of resource consumption and happiness.
