#8664. Build Muscle Without Exercise? What Science Says About Using Creatine Without Lifting

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Creatine has been around the gym long enough to have survived several generations of invention. And reinvention. And re-re-invention… Let’s just say it’s been a supplement industry staple for decades; it’s cheap, well studied, and, when combined with resistance training, actually useful. Naturally, that wasn’t sexy enough. So, now the Internet has served up a study suggesting you can take creatine, skip the gym, and build muscle anyway. The next sound in my brain after I read it was Ronnie Coleman’s voice in my head sayin’ his famous line: “Everybody wants to be a bodybuilder, but nobody wants to lift no heavy-ass weights.”

But the study is real! Researchers at Texas A&M published it in August in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, and the results have been making the rounds again this fall. I’m very familiar with the ISSN, I’ve presented at one of its conventions. I know several of the members. The organization is legit. And Texas A&M is no joke either.

Researchers recruited 73 sedentary adults between the ages of 45 and 65 for the 12-week study. Of those, 64 completed it. Some chose to follow an exercise-and-diet program. Others didn’t. Within those groups, participants were randomly assigned either ten grams of creatine monohydrate a day or a placebo.

Then this happened. The non-exercisers taking creatine gained about 2.4 pounds of lean tissue on their body-composition scans. The non-exercisers taking a placebo didn’t show the same gain. The creatine group also improved on some strength tests. So, yes, something interesting happened. But is it what we’re afraid it is?

Notice I said “lean tissue,” not two and a half pounds of brand-new muscle. The researchers used DXA scans to measure body composition. Those scans are useful, but they don’t distinguish freshly built muscle protein from all the water sitting inside lean tissue. Creatine increases water stored in muscle, especially when people first start taking it. The study didn’t directly measure changes in body water, so nobody can tell you how much of that apparent gain was actual new muscle.

There’s another detail that tends to disappear somewhere between the scientific journal and the breathless headline. The no-exercise comparison involved just thirteen creatine users and thirteen placebo users. That’s not worthless. It’s also not the population of a medium-sized city. And the researchers randomized the supplement, not the decision to exercise. Participants chose whether to join the training program, so comparisons between exercisers and non-exercisers aren’t the same as a fully randomized test of exercise itself.

The people who did train combined resistance and aerobic exercise three times a week with a calorie-restricted diet. Creatine users in that group gained nearly three pounds of lean tissue and showed greater improvements in several performance measures. That’s interesting, too, although the study can’t tell us that creatine replaces lifting. If anything, the bigger picture still favors the traditional arrangement: take the supplement if you want, but keep showing up and doing the work.

The investigators also reported some promising changes in memory tests, blood lipids, and blood-sugar markers. I’m not dismissing those findings. But they tested a lot of outcomes in a relatively small study, and the authors themselves say the individual cognitive and metabolic results are exploratory. That’s scientist speak for “hmm… now do it again with more people.”

For completeness, the study was funded by a foundation gift. A creatine manufacturer supplied the supplements and paid for one laboratory assay, and the senior researcher disclosed a position on that company’s scientific advisory board. That doesn’t make the results false. It does make disclosure worth reading, which is something every person reporting supplement research ought to do before writing a headline.

None of this changes my opinion of creatine. It’s one of the few products on the shelf with a substantial body of evidence behind it. Ten grams daily was the dose in this experiment; it doesn’t suddenly replace the more familiar 3- to 5-gram maintenance approach used by many lifters. And if you have kidney disease or other medical issues, a conversation with your clinician would be appropriate.

So can creatine help somebody who doesn’t lift? Possibly. This trial suggests it might, and that’s worth investigating. Has anybody proved that a scoop of powder builds meaningful muscle while you sit on your ass? Not from these data. The supplement is interesting precisely because it may do more than we once thought. And what we once thought was pretty damn good. We don’t have to turn it into magic dust to appreciate that.

#8663. Des Linden Finishes Ninth in Her First 100-Miler

She held the lead for several middle miles at the Javelina Jundred, but she slowed significantly after 60.

She’s been on two Olympic teams and won the Boston Marathon, but Des Linden is still a rookie when it comes to ultra events.

In her first 100-miler, the Javelina Jundred on October 31 (stretching into November 1 for some runners) in Fountain Hills, Arizona, Linden finished as the ninth woman in 16 hours and 58 minutes.

Linden ran strongly for the first three laps of the five-lap race. She took over the lead at about the 40-mile mark and held onto that lead for the next 20 miles.

She hit 60.3 miles at 8:01:12, an average of 7:58 per mile pace for more than twice the marathon distance over the hilly trails.

But at the aid station at 60.3 miles, Linden sat down while her crew tended to her. She changed shoes and took about five minutes to get up and start running again. Within a half a mile of leaving the aid station, she was walking, and two female runners, Katie Asmuth and Carla Molinaro, passed her.

The final 40 miles took her 8 hours and 57 minutes.

Although the daylight hours were primarily dry on the desert loop, heavy rain drenched the course at the start and after night fell, drawing comparisons to the 2018 Boston Marathon, which Linden won, in a nor’easter.

Heather Jackson, 42, won in 13:48:29, averaging 8:17 pace. Molinaro was second in 13:49:24, after Jackson overtook her in the final quarter mile of the race. Both earned “golden tickets” for the Western States Endurance Run, the famed 100-miler in June that goes from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California.

The men’s race was also close: Rob Molke, 35, finished in 12:11:30, holding off Noah Dusseau, who was runner-up in 12:12:57. They also earned “golden tickets” for Western States.

Linden will likely be motivated to solve the puzzle of the 100-mile distance, as she was early in her marathon career when she wanted to master 26.2 miles.

Her training wasn’t ideal leading up to Javelina, although she had several two-day stretches when she ran 30 miles one day and 20 the next.

She was aware she would need to adjust her goals if she started to struggle in the later miles.

“Just get to the finish. I think that’s super important,” she said in a phone interview with Runner’s World on October 29. “I think if I can run the whole time, that’s going to be great. And then if it’s going really well, I would love to get a golden ticket. But those are just as flexible as the plan. I know that even finishing can be something that all of a sudden comes into question. It’s just so different from anything I've done.”

Linden was also looking forward to the relaxed vibe and the chance to be around her crew and other runners.

“As a runner, you make these friends and they become your community,” she said. “But everyone lives [all over] the country. It’s hard to meet up with people, and so this is really just an excuse to hang out with a bunch of people who are really fun. It’ll be good. A good hang, no matter what.”

Sarah Lorge Butler is a writer and editor living in Eugene, Oregon, and her stories about the sport, its trends, and fascinating individuals have appeared in Runner’s World since 2005. She is the author of two popular fitness books, Run Your Butt Off! and Walk Your Butt Off!

#8662. The Comfort Crisis

As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.

In this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle. A young,excessively handsome dude who happened to be a writer with a new book out. But the headline of the episode was just intriguing enough to get me to click.

Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.

While the news headlines cry constantly about our nationwide personal debt crisis or health crisis or any other number of things that suggest that life is so hard these days, I have always seen the opposite: on average, we Americans seem to have a problem of ridiculous overindulgence and easiness in our lives, and our main problem is not recognizing it, and the damage it does to us.

So of course I had to click, and then listen to the whole two hour episode, and then buy the book, and then spend the past month reading and digesting it in small, meaningful chunks like the modern-day chunk of scripture-like wisdom that it is. And wow, am I glad I did so.

The author is Michael Easter, a former writer for Men’s Health magazine was also once catastrophically addicted to alcohol – and descended from a long family line of ancestors with the same affliction.

He was lucky to catch himself from that fall in time to save his own life, and that story alone makes the book worth reading as someone who has stood by helplessly as loved ones battled with addiction. But I think his history with overindulgence in the hollow comforts of alcohol also gives him an edge on writing about the battle between comfort and hardship on the bigger stage of life in general.

So what is The Comfort Crisis about, and how can it make all of our lives better?

The best part about this book is just what a damned good writer this Easter guy is. Like many of the most fun popular science books*, it follows a split narrative which jumps back and forth to interweave the story of an insanely difficult caribou hunting trip he joined in a remote pocket of Alaska, with the appropriate bits of science, psychology and cultural commentary that help us explain and learn from each chapter of the epic shit he had just endured. This allows us to process and apply the lessons in our own lives.

For example, have you ever wondered why the type of bored, rich suburbanites who populate the board of your local Homeowner Association and whine about unacceptably tall weeds or unauthorized skateboarding on Nextdoor are so insufferable?

Why can’t they do something better with their time?

It turns out that there’s a scientific explanation for these unfortunate people, along with most of our other problems:

The tendency of humans to always scan our environment for problems, regardless of how safe and perfect that environment is.

The book cited a study in which researchers told people to look for danger, in an environment which gradually became safer and safer:

“When they ran out of stuff to find they would start looking for a wider range of stuff, even if this was not conscious or intentional, because their job was to look for threats.”

“With that in mind, Levari recently conducted a series of studies to find out if the human brain searches for problems even when problems become infrequent or don’t exist.“

“As we experience fewer problems, we don’t become more satisfied. We just lower our threshold for what we consider a problem.“

In other words, even when our lives are virtually problem free, instead of appreciating our good fortune we just start making up shit that we can complain about instead.

And then our politicians cock their greasy, finely-tuned ears in our direction and make up policies to appease our mostly-insubstantial concerns. And they invent their own trivial “wedge” issues to get us to all bicker about our different cultures and religions, suddenly caring about things that would not have even been problems if nobody told us they were.

And there’s America’s weakness in a nutshell, and meanwhile our strength comes entirely from the times we choose not to waste our time stooping to this level.

Meanwhile, the opposite effect holds true: people who survive in rougher environments than us end up more resilient and less prone to complaining.

In a series of recent interviews, Ukrainian people living in the war zones of their occupied country were asked “is it safe to live where you live?” and a strangely high percentage still said “Yes” – not all that different from the responses of US residents when asked the same question about their own cities.

This adaptation principle also explains why some first generation immigrants tend to build businesses and wealth while their own offspring in second and third generations are more likely to become complacent and spend it down. As an immigrant myself, I can see why this is: conditions were just slightly more harsh and less comfortable and wealthy where I grew up, so I adapted to those conditions as “normal” which made the United States seem posh and easy by comparison. Which made it easier to spend less money and accumulate more.

The trap of pointless worry is just one of the many revelations of The Comfort Crisis. It also gives insightful explanations for why spending time in Nature boosts our mental and physical health, while cubicles and car driving grind us down.

There’s something in our biological wiring that responds instantly and powerfully to everything natural, in ways that you can’t get anywhere else.

Even placing a single plant into a hospital room will measurably improve the recovery of almost all patients from almost all ailments. So can you imagine the power of the medicine you are inhaling if you step into a real, living forest? And what if you spent several hours there, or even several days?

Later, we get lessons on our human adaptation towards the ratio of effort to reward:

And our bizarre natural aversion to physical exertion:

Which is remarkable, given the absolutely insane cost this tendency imposes upon us.

Moving your body, even a bit, has enormous benefits – again to almost all people towards reducing the probability and severity of almost all diseases. So can you imagine the benefit of moving your body for several hours per day in a natural environment, and including heavy load bearing and bits of extreme exertion?

These things are not speculative pieces of alternative medicine. They are known, easily and reproducibly tested, and proven to be the most effective things we can possibly do with our time.

So why, the actual fuck, are people still sitting inside, watching Netflix, driving to work, and then driving to the doctor’s office to get deeper and deeper analysis of a neverending series of exotic and mysterious and unsolvable problems with their physical and mental health?

We should at least start with the stuff we know is essential – maximum outdoor time every day, heavy exertion including with weights, minimal time spent sitting and driving, and minimum junk food, sugar, and alcohol. You definitely don’t have to be perfect, but just understand that these are the big levers for physical and mental health.

Only then, once you reach these minimum basic things for human survival, should you expect that more exotic and niche medicines and treatments are the only course of action.

By all means, follow your doctor’s orders and don’t just dump all of your medications down the sink because of this MMM rant. But at the same time, realize that the stuff that is hard and uncomfortable is very likely to be the stuff that improves your life the most.

It’s all the stuff that Mr. Money Mustache has been telling you since 2012, but with more detail and less distraction. This book is a concentrated packet of advice for solid living.

In a happy coincidence, I happened to be in the middle of some hard stuff** of my own as I worked my way through The Comfort Crisis and I found the perspective quite useful and transformative to apply hot off the press.

Normally somewhat of a homebody, I had embarked on a solo journey for some Carpentourism deep in the mountains of Southwestern Colorado. I had my whole life shrunk down into the new Model Y including food, bed, and the necessary tools and materials to tackle a pretty long laundry list of tasks on two different construction projects (fixing up a mini-resort property in Salida, and starting construction on a small cabin in Durango)

The trip immediately took a turn towards the dramatic as I climbed into the mountains and drove straight into the most torrential rainstorm I have ever seen, then accidentally broke a traffic law in a remote mountain town right in front of both of the local police officers ($115 fine and two points off my license), then five minutes after that had a small pebble hit my brand-new windshield which instantly spread into a crack that spans the whole thing, all before finally limping into Salida to unpack and get started on the work.

“Big deal”, I can already hear you saying, “Retired man experiences two minor incidents while taking a vacation in his luxury car.”

And you’re right, and that is exactly my point.

My life is so stable and comfortable that even these two miniature challenges threw me off balance, and I arrived in a slightly bummed and stressed-out state. But I still knew that in the bigger picture, they are good for me if I accept them as the lessons they are rather than choosing to continue to worry about them.

As the trip went on, more things happened, almost as if The Comfort Crisis book were trying to prove a point. I drove three hours deeper into the mountains and up the steep dirt road to arrive at my second friend’s piece of land – a plot of forest in the mountains just outside of Durango.

My work days in that high desert environment in the peak of summer were hot and physically demanding. It was hard to keep my tools, and my food supply in the cooler, and myself protected from the scorching sun (and a strange neverending blizzard of tree pollen) while still getting the job done. There was no indoor plumbing and we had to be very careful with our limited water supply. And then at the end of each day I had to reshuffle everything and set my car back up as a bedroom and crawl in for the night. Alone and far from home.

But instead of feeling depressed as I experienced this constant hardship, the opposite thing was happening: I felt more alive and more badass with each passing day. I got better at being a feral forest man.

One day, my co-builder and I decided to take the afternoon off and head to the wild, remote Lemon Reservoir for some paddleboarding. We didn’t bring our phones or any other conveniences or amenities – just two boards and the minimal clothing required for swimming. And we headed out into a stiff headwind and little whitecap waves, laughing at the freedom of the experience.

It was hard, and slightly scary, as we got further and further from the shore. Progress was slow even with serious paddling, and we didn’t have any particular plan beyond the spirit of “let’s GO!”

But again Michael Easter was there whispering in my ear, saying,

“Is this difficult, Mustache? GOOOOoood! Then you’d better keep going!”

So we did. And we got way out into that lake, to a point where the water was shielded from the wind by the mountains on the other side. And it was awesome.

We cruised over to the shore to explore a particularly scenic meadow, coated with the softest green mossy grass and exuberantly colored wildflowers, and set at an impossibly steep angle. And damn I wished that I could have taken pictures, but in a strange way this forced me to burn that spot more thoroughly into my memories using my own senses instead.

Then we headed back out into the center of the lake, set down the paddles, and just laid down on our boards to let the wind and the waves take us back towards the far end of the lake where we had started. And what a strange, serene feeling it was, floating on just a tube of air over two hundred feet of cold blue water, feeling like a jungle man with no cares and no plans and no material possessions. It could have been scary, but instead it was one of the best and most relaxed moments of my life.

Eventually, this week of forest living and exertion had to come to an end so I could get back to my own town to be a Dad again. But it ended with a final reminder of the principles of the Comfort Crisis – after so many days relatively extreme work and a relatively sparse food supply, I had grown used to a healthy background hunger. Which is yet another thing that we are meant to experience as humans – being satisfied and free from hunger all the time is neither normal nor healthy.

But when my hosts took me out on the town for a final night thank you dinner at the Mexican restaurant, the immense Burrito platter I consumed turned out to be the most delicious meal of my life.

Purposeful Hardship vs. Purposeful Spending

There has been a lot of talk directed at the FIRE community recently about how bad we are at spending our money, and how we all need to loosen up. And there’s a small amount of truth to it, as my local friends Carl and Mindy recently admitted during a grilling on the Ramit Sethi podcast.

But we also need to keep this whole idea of excessive comfort in mind, and the damage it does to the natural human condition.

It’s great to spend money on adventures and improving yourself, being generous to others, and making the world a better place.

But it’s also way too easy to fool yourself into thinking you “want” things that just make your life easier and easier.

So your job is to catch yourself before this happens, and learn to keep things challenging, even as you upgrade the rest of your life experience.

In other words: buy yourself better tools, not softer chairs.

* Another great book that follows this style is Wired for Love by neruroscientist Stephanie Cacioppo – highly recommended for reading in parallel with a lover, whether new or old.

** not actually hard by reasonable human standards, but it seemed hard by my comfort addicted first world standards

For me, the questions that help me decide which “jobs” are worth doing for life include these ones: – Would I still keep doing this job for life, even if I didn’t get paid for it? – Does this job contribute to my physical and emotional health? (positive contact with other humans, plus physical exertion outdoors) – Does the job allow enough time flexibility or time off that I can also take care of myself and those around me? (8 hours of sleep with no alarm clock, time to spend with your kids or travel to take care of your aging family members, etc)

If all these things apply, it may well be a good job regardless of how hard it is.

If few or none of them apply, there is still good news: there are lots of jobs that DO offer these things. Especially thanks to the power of self employment.

One thing my family did that most people find crazy is to get rid of most of our seating furniture. We ditched one couch, two armchairs, one chair-and-a-half, one upholstered ottoman, and six dining room tables. We also lowered our table and replaced our conventional beds with wool pads on the floor.

Now we sit and sleep on the floor for the most part. It’s encouraged us to move our bodies more (lots of floor space means room for stretching and exercising) and getting down to the floor to sit or sleep (and then getting back up again) means lots of movement that strengthens our legs. My sister in particular thinks this is verging on child abuse and most of my friends just think we’re nuts. But this is a normal way to live in much of the world; we just find it odd because our culture says it’s not how it should be done.

It was difficult at first, and sure, a nice cushy couch still feels good to me (for about five minutes), but it’s amazing how quickly you start to crave things that require more effort once you change your mindset about it.

Great article, I’ve been following this blog for years but have never commented before. I thought I’d share, as I have always felt that I have the perfect job for the younger mustachians out there looking for ways to challenge themselves in this vein while building wealth. An Interagency Hotshot Crew is a group of 20 wildland firefighters that travel across the western U.S., Alaska, and sometimes Canada to work on large wildfires. It is almost exclusively hard manual labor for long hours over difficult terrain and conditions. It will push most young folks past what they thought they were capable of, and a dedication to physical fitness is a requirement of the job. Spending months with the same group of like minded people doing difficult things with a sense of purpose builds strong comradery and incredible friendships. You get to see many of the most beautiful parts of the country, and experience the impressive power of the natural world. You are basically living for free half of the year, as your meals are provided and you sleep on the ground. I can still remember the first time I ate a low-grade steak over a campfire after working 16 hours, it was the most delicious meal I’ve ever had. “Hunger is the best seasoning”, as one of my crewmembers liked to put it. After a long season (1000 + hours of overtime), newer folks get the entire winter off. If you leverage your free time and fire checks wisely, you can drastically improve your situation while staying debt free. I was able to finish college, do some travelling, and build my house, all while saving money. It’s definitely not for everyone, and I don’t know if I would recommend it for a long career as the schedule doesn’t lend itself to a very balanced lifestyle. But for someone in their 20s looking to challenge themselves, I’ve always felt it is an amazing job.

Interesting conversation. One thing I didn’t see anyone mention is the fact that humans, like virtually all other mammals, are hard-wired to do as little as possible outside of the necessities (finding food, shelter, fornicating, fighting enemies) because energy expended on activities not related to those necessary for survival may just cost one their survival, at least in the “old days” of the jungle. The same evolutionary factors that make our bodies not want to shed fat or what to eat (sweet, not bitter) are in play when deciding whether to take the stairs or the escalator. It’s highly likely that without the default of lazy that most of what makes up civilization wouldn’t exist, since virtually everything we’ve ever invented beyond ensuring basic survival has been to reduce energy expenditure. Why walk when you can drive? Why forage when you can farm? ETC.

So the human animal has to consciously make the decision to do that which goes against his/her basic instincts.

A great book about it: “Exercised: The Science of Physical Activity, Rest and Health”, by Daniel E. Lieberman.

The members of Five Finger Death Punch have been busy lately. Their 10th studio album, Legacy, was recently released, and they began their 20th Anniversary World Tour in July with the North American leg. Zoltán Báthory is the founder of 5FDP as well as their rhythm guitarist and primary songwriter. When asked his thoughts about celebrating two decades of success, Báthory was proud but more grateful for their legions of fans.

“It was always the people’s band,” he said with a smile. The Las Vegas band has been around so long, they were first getting attention on MySpace. Báthory recalled experts writing in magazines that they wouldn’t be around very long, but staying true to themselves and focusing only on the music has been their key to success.

“We just kept pushing and the people stayed with us.”

Báthory knows their music is not for everybody, but he hears stories all the time from people who have told them that hits such as “Under and Over It” and “Wash it All Away” are on their workout playlists or may have helped them get past a hard time in their lives. Báthory views that as a badge of honor because he himself trains in Flex Lewis’ Dragon Lair gym in Las Vegas and is as much a part of that community as he is the hard rock and heavy metal space.

“I’m proud of that because these are my people.”

5FDP also has a large following in the military and first responder communities. Aside from their many hits, they are known for their support of veterans and firefighters through donations to the Call of Duty Endowment fund, doing other fundraisers through their music, and Báthory has served on boards for groups like the Home Deployment Project.

“When I get a military guy telling me, ‘It’s difficult to be in a war zone. But I got up every day and listened to you guys, and it not just got me ready for the day, it got me through the day.’ That kind of gives us a justification that we’re doing something good. So, it also keeps us going. I love it.”

Báthory’s love for music and working out may only be rivaled by his passion for judo. Growing up in Hungary, judo in his home country was more popular than it is in North America. He first started following the discipline at age 9 and was entering tournaments before becoming a teenager. Báthory felt that taking up judo has done far more for him than improving his skills alone.

“I can say and I can claim that that philosophy of judo was one of the key elements of me becoming successful,” he explained. “It rewires your mind, and you start to think very differently.”

Báthory still makes time to train and actively competes in tournaments to this day. He has also taken up jiujitsu and reports having black belts in both disciplines. But he is not only trying to be better in martial arts but for it as well. Judo is an Olympic sport, and athletes internationally are very committed to excelling in it. The American judo scene is not as prominent as it is in other countries, but Báthory is trying to change that and wants to help those Americans looking to compete in the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles, California.

“I’ve worked with USA Judo and IJF (International Judo Federation). It’s one of my missions to make judo more visible in America, for more people to practice it.”

Báthory’s passion and commitment to his mission is more than moral support and advocacy. He has even made a financial commitment to this goal.

“I want the American team to do really well in judo. I’m even financially supporting the judo team. A portion of the tickets of this tour is actually going to USA Judo so they can afford the participation in training camps.”

Even though they have two decades behind them, 5FDP is as popular as ever, and tickets to their shows have already been selling fast. Like any elite band, they have had their shares of growing pains and critics, but the loyal fanbase and joy they get from creating music and performing it continues to fuel their desire.

Báthory has as much love and appreciation for their supporters as they do for the band. That’s because of the communities those fans are in; military, first responders, athletes, martial arts, and others who are looking for something positive to lean on. Báthory proclaimed that 5FDP will continue to make music and do their best to support their fans not only because they support them but because of what they do.

“What is the common denominator between these people? They all help other people.”

You can learn more about 5FDP, their tour, and Legacy by going to their website and subscribing to their YouTube channel.

Follow Báthory on Instagram @zoltanbathory and @zoltanbjj.

#8659. Texas A&M Study Shows Creatine Adding Muscle Mass Gains Without Lifting

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

For better brain cognition through to superior strength and power, creatine is one of those supplements that seems to actually work. Thanks to its cell volumizing and energizing abilities, creatine allows us to lift heavier, recover faster, and focus better under stress. Now, a new study from Texas A&M University is touting that creatine can construct more muscle even without a structured resistance training program.

The study, published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, suggests that creatine could help adults to maintain lean tissue and strength, even without regular exercise. Of course, maintaining adequate levels of muscle mass is particularly important as we age because muscle loss, also known as sarcopenia, can begin as early as 35 years, and typically sees lean mass decline at a rate of 1 to 2 percent, per year, for the average person. In fact, those who fail to engage with regular resistance training could lose as much as 4 to 6 pounds of muscle per decade.

New meta-analyses show this tried and true supp can benefit both men and women—but you still have to...

For 12 weeks, men and women between the ages of 45 and 65 were provided with creatine or a maltodextrin placebo, with each group being split into those who wanted to participate in a supervised, structured exercise program, and those who didn’t want to commit to the organized sessions. As the participants filled out questionnaires during the study, data showed that the structured exercise group racked up more moderate-to-vigorous activity than those who weren’t locked in.

Despite lower levels of activity, those who took two 5g doses of creatine per day, and were not in the structured exercise program, increased their lean tissue by around 2.4 pounds over the 12-week study period. Conversely, those who took the placebo lost almost half a pound. “Creatine Monohydrate supplementation without exercise training and diet intervention increased lean tissue mass, strength, and muscular endurance while promoting favorable changes in selected blood lipids, HbA1c, and selected markers of cognitive function and memory,” read the report.

The results on muscle mass were even more profound in the structured exercise group, however. Creatine users who undertook the supervised sessions gained 2.8 pounds of lean mass on average. Creatine was also shown to preserve muscle even under the conditions of fat loss, because participants in the exercise program were given a modest calorie deficit. After 12 weeks, this group had gained almost three pounds of lean tissue despite dropping fat, while the exercise group that took a placebo showed little change in lean tissue. Still, both the structured and non-structured groups, on creatine, saw a greater reduction in body fat percentage than that seen by exercise or diet alone.

“Creatine Monohydrate supplementation with and without exercise and diet intervention may help middle-aged and older adults maintain muscle mass and strength while favorably affecting selected markers of health and cognitive function,” concluded the study.

Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. Cathay Pacific consistently ranks among the world's top airlines for business class. The A350-1000 is their flagship long-haul aircraft, featuring a 1-2-1 configuration with every single seat having direct aisle access. There are no middle seats. There are no awkward climbs over sleeping strangers. There is a full dine-on-demand menu, a curated wine list, noise-canceling headphones, and a ground service team that treats you like a valued guest before you even board. For the FI traveler, this redemption represents something rare: a genuine luxury experience — the kind that recalibrates your sense of what travel can feel like — made nearly free through a well-understood system. The math works. The experience delivers. And once you've done it, you'll understand exactly why the ChooseFI community talks about this one.

Alaska Mileage Plan is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. The secret is their partner award chart: Alaska uses fixed pricing for partner airline awards, meaning costs do not fluctuate with demand the way dynamic programs do. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Alaska has partnerships with Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Japan Airlines, Emirates, Fiji Airways, and others. The primary way to earn Alaska miles is through the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card (Bank of America), through flying, or via Marriott Bonvoy transfers at a 3:1 ratio.

Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. This is the pricing inefficiency at the heart of this redemption, and it's why the ChooseFI community treats Alaska Mileage Plan as one of the most valuable programs in the industry.

Alaska Mileage Plan has only one meaningful transfer partner for most people: Marriott Bonvoy, at a ratio of 3 Bonvoy points to 1 Alaska mile. That's a steep ratio — you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points to generate 55,000 Alaska miles — and transfer times run 1 to 5 days, so plan accordingly. There is no direct credit card transfer path into Alaska Mileage Plan from Chase, Amex, or Citi, which is why the "Easy to Earn" score for this redemption is a 2 out of 5. The miles must be earned directly: through Alaska's co-branded credit card (the Alaska Airlines Visa from Bank of America), through flying Alaska or its partners, or via Marriott transfer.

This is crucial and often overlooked. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on any partner award bookings. This matters enormously for a Cathay Pacific redemption. If you were to book the same Cathay flight through Cathay's own Asia Miles program or through British Airways Avios, you could face fuel surcharges of $400–$900 or more on top of the points cost. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket cost is taxes and fees only — typically in the range of $50–$150 depending on the routing. That's it. A $12,000 experience for 55,000 miles and roughly $100 in fees.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit that is genuinely rare among U.S. programs. On the LAX–HKG–SYD routing, this means you can build a stopover in Hong Kong at no additional points cost. Spend a few days exploring one of the world's most dynamic cities — the markets of Mong Kok, the skyline from Victoria Peak, the dim sum temples of Kowloon — then board your continuing flight to Sydney. Two destinations. One redemption. Same 55,000 miles.

The 55,000-mile rate applies to both Cathay Pacific and Qantas for business class to Australia. Cathay routes you through Hong Kong (HKG); Qantas has its own metal and routing options. If Cathay availability is thin, checking Qantas can open up alternatives without changing your points cost.

Do not start at Alaska's website. Alaska's own search tool for partner availability can be unreliable for Cathay Pacific. Instead, go to ba.com (British Airways' booking site) and run a one-way business class search for your desired route — for example, LAX to SYD or LAX to HKG. British Airways and Cathay Pacific are oneworld partners, and BA's search engine surfaces Cathay award availability with remarkable accuracy. Look for "Reward" seats in the business class (Club World or equivalent) cabin. Any dates showing availability on BA.com are almost certainly bookable through Alaska as well. Screenshot or note the specific dates before moving on.

Alaska opens its award booking window 331 days in advance. If you're targeting peak travel dates — Australian summer (December–February), for example — set a calendar reminder to search and transfer 331 days ahead. Your miles also never expire in Mileage Plan, which gives you flexibility to accumulate without pressure.

Confirm you have at least 55,000 Alaska miles available. If you're converting Marriott Bonvoy points, you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points at the 3:1 ratio. Initiate transfers at least one week before you plan to call, as Marriott-to-Alaska transfers can take 1 to 5 days.

Log into your Marriott Bonvoy account, navigate to "Transfer Points," select Alaska Airlines as the recipient program, and enter your Mileage Plan number. Transfer in increments of 3,000 Bonvoy points (yielding 1,000 Alaska miles). Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1 — points transfers are generally non-reversible.

This redemption cannot be booked online — Alaska's web portal does not support all partner award bookings, particularly for Cathay Pacific. Call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522. Tell the agent:

Have your Mileage Plan number, passport information, and a credit card for the taxes and fees ready. The call typically takes 20–40 minutes. Agents are generally knowledgeable, but if you encounter confusion, politely ask for a senior agent or call back.

If Cathay availability is limited on your preferred dates, ask the agent to check Qantas availability to Australia at the same 55,000-mile rate. Qantas Business (The Business) has its own award inventory and may have open seats when Cathay is fully allocated.

If you're routing through Hong Kong on Cathay, explicitly ask the agent to add a free stopover at HKG. This is a program benefit, not a favor — Alaska's routing rules allow one free stopover on one-way awards. Specify how many nights you want in Hong Kong before the continuing flight to Sydney.

The best way to find Cathay Pacific Business Class award availability is through the British Airways website (ba.com). Search for one-way flights from your U.S. gateway to Sydney or Melbourne, and look for dates showing Cathay Pacific-operated flights with Business Class availability. British Airways shows oneworld partner availability more reliably than most tools.

If Cathay Pacific shows no availability on your preferred dates, search for Qantas Business Class on the same route. Qantas availability can be found through the Qantas website or through British Airways. The Alaska Mileage Plan price is the same 55,000 miles for either carrier.

Earn miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa card sign-up bonus (typically 60,000 to 75,000 miles), through flying Alaska or partners, or by transferring from Marriott Bonvoy. If transferring from Marriott, allow 1 to 5 business days for the transfer to complete before your booking window closes.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522 and request a partner award booking on Cathay Pacific (or Qantas) Business Class. Provide your desired dates and routing. Ask about adding a free stopover in Hong Kong if routing through HKG. The agent will process the booking and deduct 55,000 miles plus taxes and fees (typically $50 to $150).

After booking through Alaska, manage your seat selection directly through the Cathay Pacific website or app using your booking reference. Select a window or aisle seat in the 1-2-1 configuration — every seat has direct aisle access, so there is no wrong choice. You can also pre-order meals and manage other preferences through Cathay's platform.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

#8655. Common Reasons Diets Stop Working After a While

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Early progress on a weight-loss plan can give way to a stretch where the same effort no longer produces the same results. That shift reflects a set of predictable physiological and behavioral forces that push back against restrictive eating.

Below are nine of those forces and how each one slows progress.

As body weight drops, the body burns fewer calories at rest, partly because it starts conserving energy.

Researchers call this adaptive thermogenesis. A 2026 randomized trial published in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics detected it within the first week of reduced energy intake. Over time, the same plan produces less progress, even when effort stays consistent.

Weight loss pushes appetite in the wrong direction.

As the body’s energy stores shrink, hunger increases and meals feel less filling. Steeper cuts in food intake intensify both signals, and that pressure makes aggressive restriction hard to sustain.

Banning a food intensifies the desire for it. Eliminating a food works against established habits and social life at the same time, so the plan ends and the banned foods return.

Restrictive weight loss draws energy from muscle as well as fat. Muscle burns energy even at rest, so losing it lowers metabolism further.

A 2025 paper from Reviews in Endocrine & Metabolic Disorders reports that regained weight disproportionately returns as fat rather than as the lean tissue that was lost. The method of weight loss influences how much muscle the body keeps.

In a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial published in Obesity Science & Practice, participants on the Trilivy™ Reset 5 & 1 Plan retained 98% of lean mass and reduced visceral fat by 14% over 16 weeks.*

“A weight management program that protects lean mass, reduces visceral fat, and builds habit infrastructure is designed for the years after the active weight loss phase and addresses the conditions that drive regain at the source,” said Satya Jonnalagadda, PhD, MBA, RD, Vice President, Scientific & Clinical Affairs at Trilivy.

Constant restriction demands steady mental effort, and a single stressful event can be enough to derail a plan.

Coaching gives people support to continue their plan through stressful periods.

In the same trial from Obesity Science & Practice, participants with coach support lost up to 10 times more weight and 17 times more fat than those in a self-directed group. Trilivy coaches provide accountability and real-time support that help keep a plan on track.

“In a world of automation and AI, human connection is our superpower,” Jonnalagadda said. “A coach can meet a person in the exact moment a routine breaks down, and that is something a notification has never been able to do.”

A pass-fail approach to eating leaves no room for an imperfect meal. Under that framework, deviation from a meal plan feels like a reason to stop, and each restart interrupts the consistency that progress builds on.

Small, untracked additions, like a slightly larger serving or a few bites while cooking, add energy without registering as a meal. Weight loss also prompts the body to reduce spontaneous movement, which lowers daily energy use.

Both shifts happen gradually, and together they slow progress.

In a 2026 study from Annals of Internal Medicine, adults who slept about 80 minutes less per night gained roughly a pound and became more sedentary over six weeks. Their weight gain tracked closely with the drop in daily movement.

The finding connects short sleep to reduced activity, one of the everyday inputs a weight-loss plan relies on.

Restaurant meals, birthdays, work events, and holidays bring menus, timing and traditions that differ from an established meal plan.

Rules designed around a home kitchen do not offer guidance for those moments. A plan that accounts for eating out and celebrations gives people a way to navigate them.

Each of these nine factors traces back to two pressures: a body that works to protect its energy stores and daily routines that strict rules don’t account for.

A sustainable approach to weight management addresses both. It protects lean muscle, pairs balanced nutrition and physical activity with healthy daily habits, and builds in coaching and accountability that continue past the initial results, supporting long-term metabolic health.

Trilivy™ recommends that you contact your healthcare provider before starting and throughout your weight loss journey.

* Arterburn LM, et al. Randomized controlled trial assessing two commercial weight loss programs in adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity Science & Practice. 2019. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/osp4.312. In a clinical study, individuals on the Reset 5 & 1 Plan experienced a reduction of 14% visceral fat and 98% of lean mass was retained at 16 weeks. Those on the Reset 5 & 1 Plan with the support of a coach lost up to 10x more weight and 17x more fat than those who tried to lose weight on their own.

#8653. This Self-Coached Data Scientist Had Never Run a Marathon Before. Then He Won NYC.

Andreas Almgren made his marathon debut on the streets of New York this weekend—and he won in 2:06:01.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published on October 27, 2026. At the NYC Marathon on November 1, Almgren gapped the field and won the race in 2:06:01.

When the elites line up for the New York City Marathon on November 1, there will be a mix of former winners, Olympic medalists, and two of the top American marathoners in the country, Conner Mantz and Zouhair Talbi.

Looking to spoil the party will be Andreas Almgren, a 31-year-old Swedish runner who won the World Half Marathon Championships in September. This will be Almgren’s debut at the 26.2-mile distance. Despite his inexperience, he’s a legitimate threat for the podium.

Almgren has an unconventional background as a pro runner. He was working as a data scientist just two years ago. He mostly trains alone and coaches himself. But he’s far from a competitive amateur. He’s sponsored by Nike and has set European records in the road 10K (26:45) and half marathon (58:06).

Although his strengths have been on the track and shorter road events, Almgren has leaned fully into marathon training this fall, logging more than 135 miles a week and tackling long runs over 24 miles. He says he’s well-prepared heading into New York.

“I’m actually feeling really confident,” Almgren told Runner’s World ahead of the race. “I might be a bit naive, but the training has gone really well. I’ve done a few really good workouts. But the marathon is a different beast. You don’t really know until you're reaching that 35K mark if you're going to make it or not. But I’m feeling really good.”

Here are six things to know about Almgren ahead of his marathon debut in New York City.

Almgren first made a splash on the world scene as an 800-meter specialist, earning bronze in the event at the World Junior Championships in 2014. For about a decade, he was coached by Urban Aruhn, but around 2019, Almgren began experimenting with Norwegian threshold training and gradually started to create his own training plans.

Aruhn is still involved today, but in a more general role. Before a training cycle, Almgren will run his plan by Aruhn, who plays “devil’s advocate,” trying to poke holes in it or prod Almgren to explain his reasoning.

“If we disagree on something, then we discuss it,” Almgren said. “But in the end, it’s in my hands.”

Before he was a full-time professional runner, Almgren worked as a risk analyst at a financial company and then as a data scientist for the sports tech software company Svexa. It wasn’t until he was sidelined from the 2024 Olympics with a stress fracture that he decided to quit his job and focus on running full-time.

Now, Almgren—who has a bachelor’s degree in industrial engineering and management and has taken graduate coursework in mathematics, optimization, and systems theory—scratches that itch by rigorously tracking his training metrics.

“I like data,” he said. “And I collect basically the things that I think are important for every workout.”

Almgren has an Excel spreadsheet where he logs every workout and numerous data points: interval times, heart rate readings, blood lactate measurements, etc. The spreadsheet data goes back to 2012, and Almgren will look back on past sessions to inform his current training.

Almgren has been preparing for New York with an altitude stint in Flagstaff, Arizona, which sits 7,000 feet above sea level. He’s also introduced heat training during some of his training blocks, and he looks to sports like cycling and speed skating for cutting-edge training methods.

About two years ago, Almgren started experimenting with Nomio, a broccoli sprout extract shot that is quickly catching on among elite runners. Nomio claims the product can reduce lactate during hard efforts and accelerate recovery.

Almgren, who is sponsored by the brand, said it helps keep his legs feeling fresh during intervals.

“I just feel like I can train harder than I did before and more and still recover from it,” he said. “Run a little bit faster on my threshold workouts and everything. So I think if you get those tiny margins over and over, day by day, I think that could help quite a lot.”

Almgren knew he wanted to race a marathon in the fall of 2026, but he didn’t want to sacrifice a full track season before diving into marathon training. He chose New York because it gave him time to recover from the track season, and he wanted to find an honest race, compared to a more time-oriented flat course like Spain’s Valencia Marathon in December.

“In a time trial, I wouldn’t really know what time to aim for,” Almgren said. “There’s a big risk that I blow up. If I’m going in Valencia, you have Yomif [Kejelcha] and John Korir taking off in probably sub-two-hour pace, and I’m not going to follow that. So I think that New York is a better race for me with inexperience, just trying to stay in the front pack and see what can happen.”

Oftentimes, pro runners will “move to the marathon,” implying their days of barreling around the track are over. But Almgren wants to do both. He fully intends to run a track season in 2027, and, looking ahead to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, he believes the 10,000 meters could be his best event.

If Almgren finishes in the top five at New York, he will earn the Olympic standard and pave the path for a spot on the Swedish marathon team for the upcoming Games.

Only Emil Zatopek has won gold in the 10,000 meters and marathon at the same Olympics.

Like most elite runners who race the hilly New York course, Almgren doesn’t care what his finishing time is on November 1. Instead, he wants to run with the top group as long as he can.

“The goal is to be in the mindset that I should try to be able to compete for the whole race,” he said. “I don't want to, let’s say, chicken out at 30K. I want to try to be in it for as long as possible. And if that means that I blow up at 37K, then so be it.

“But I hope that I should be able to be in the mix up until Central Park and hopefully even maybe come out on top. We’ll see. You should never underestimate a marathon. And I don’t have the experience, so I don’t know what’s going to happen, but I’m going to try to be in the mix.”

Theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.)

#8651. In His First Marathon, Andreas Almgren Stuns the Field to Win the New York City Marathon

The Swede raced like a veteran, breaking the tape in 2:06:01.

In his debut at the distance, Andreas Almgren ran today’s New York City Marathon like a veteran, perfectly marshaling his energy for one big move in the final mile to win in 2:06:01. The Swede is the first European-born man to win the race since Giacomo Leone in 1996.

Yeman Crippa of Italy, who was the last to hang with Almgren, placed second in 2:06:14 (and then promptly vomited). Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho outkicked defending champion Benson Kipruto in the final meters to finish third in a personal best of 2:06:26, one second ahead of Kipruto.

Zouhair Talbi, who occasionally took the lead between halfway and 30K (18.6 miles), was the top U.S. finisher, placing sixth in 2:06:43. In his debut marathon, Ahmed Muhumed was the second American, finishing seventh in 2:07:02. Ryan Ford was the third U.S. finisher, placing 10th in 2:07:17. Conner Mantz, running his first marathon since setting the U.S. record last year in Chicago, was 11th in 2:07:27.

Almgren is a world-class track runner—he won bronze at 10,000 meters at last year’s world championships—who has quickly also mastered road racing. Six weeks ago, he won the world half marathon championship in a national record of 58:06. He even boasts an 800-meter best of 1:45, a borderline world-class time that none of his competitors has run.

Despite that pedigree, none of the seasoned marathoners made a serious effort to drop Almgren far out from the finish. Fifteen men remained bunched at the 35K (21.7 miles) mark.

The real racing didn’t start until defending champ Kipruto surged to a 4:38 24th mile. That led to him, Almgren, and Crippa separating. Almgren, who trains by kilometers instead of miles, waited until just before 40K (24.9 miles) to take the lead for the first time. Crippa was able to stick with him for another kilometer, but right as Crippa snuck a look back on Central Park South, Almgren surged again and ran unchallenged to the finish.

When asked after the race whether he thought the moderate first 30 kilometers was playing into his hands, Almgren said, “Kinda, but not really. I mean, this is my first marathon. I don’t really know how it’s supposed to feel at those different points.”

At 20 miles, Almgren said, “I was like, ‘Shit, I’m tired. Why are my legs feeling like this?’” But a few minutes later, “I just started feeling like, ‘It’s pretty easy to respond now to the moves.’ So somewhere around there I felt like, ‘Okay, this might be my day.’”

Known as a meticulous planner and trainer, Almgren watched last year’s marathon from three spots—from mile 8 in Brooklyn, in the 17th mile along First Avenue in Manhattan, and near the finish in Central Park. That evening, he texted his manager that he wanted to race here this year.

Almgren earned $100,000 for the win, with Crippa and Mofolo getting $60,000 and $40,000, respectively, for placing second and third. Talbi earned $25,000 for being the first U.S. finisher.

Mofolo might especially enjoy his earnings, given that today is his 21st birthday and he can now legally visit a tavern or two should the mood strike. He’s one to keep an eye on. He debuted at Cape Town in May, placing 11th in 2:08:50, and not only improved significantly but ran fearlessly, even taking a brief solo lead around the 20-mile mark.

For what was such a moderate race early on, with the leaders passing halfway between 64:01 and 64:04, the finishing times significantly rewrote the event’s all-time performance list. Almgren’s 2:06:01 ties the fourth fastest in race history, and Crippa, Mofolo, Kipruto, Haftu Strintzos (fifth in 2:06:34), and Talbi are also now in the top ten.
